napoli-in-3-giorni.content: Three days is the right amount of Naples. With one day you rush; with a week you start living here. Three days let you take things slowly: two for the city, one to get out. The bay is worth as much as Naples itself, and going home without seeing Pompeii, an island or the Amalfi Coast would be a shame.

You don’t need a car; in fact you’re better off without one. The old centre is walkable, you ride a funicular (a cable railway up the hill) to the Vomero, and the metro does the rest. Below you’ll find what to see in Naples in 3 days, day by day, then where to stay, how to get around and what’s worth booking before you leave.
Day 1: the old centre and underground
The first day fits into a single square kilometre: churches, cloisters, workshops, alleys, and under your feet the Greek and Roman city. Comfortable shoes, and no minute-by-minute schedule.
Morning: Spaccanapoli, Santa Chiara and the Veiled Christ

Start at Piazza del Gesù. Round the corner is the majolica-tiled cloister of Santa Chiara, the quietest spot of the day: best seen early. Then head into Spaccanapoli, the dead-straight street that cuts the old centre in two and, seen from the Vomero, looks like a crack in the city. Walk it without a map, past San Domenico Maggiore; getting lost is part of the game.

The Cappella Sansevero is right next door. Inside is the Cristo Velato (Veiled Christ), carved by Giuseppe Sanmartino in 1753: a marble Christ under a veil that looks like real fabric. You walk around the statue in silence, then go down to the anatomical machines, two skeletons with their circulatory systems on display. The chapel is small and always full, and you need your ticket in advance: without a booking the queue can eat half your day. End the morning on San Gregorio Armeno, the street of nativity-scene workshops, with the Duomo (the cathedral) a few steps away.
The Veiled Christ sets the shape of the day. Book your chapel time slot first, then build the rest around it: Santa Chiara before, San Gregorio Armeno after.
Lunch: pizza

By lunchtime you’re between Via dei Tribunali and Via Duomo, which is exactly the right place. The pizzerias in the centre almost always have a queue outside. Two options: sit down early, or get a pizza a portafoglio, a “wallet pizza” folded into quarters in paper, to eat as you walk. Skip the starters: Neapolitan pizza is big and the afternoon is long.
Afternoon: the MANN or underground

Here you have to choose, because both won’t fit. Option one is the National Archaeological Museum, the MANN: the mosaics from the House of the Faun, the bronzes from the Villa of the Papyri, the Farnese Bull and the Farnese Hercules, the Secret Cabinet. If you’re going to Pompeii or Herculaneum on day three, this is the afternoon for it, because the best of what came out of the excavations is here. The museum is huge, and on your own you leave exhausted.

Option two is Naples below ground: cisterns, tunnels and air-raid shelters dug into the tuff, the soft volcanic stone the city stands on. In the old centre you go down into the Greek and Roman city; under the Quartieri Spagnoli (the Spanish Quarter) you reach forty metres deep. The most unusual is the Galleria Borbonica, under Chiaia. Ferdinand II had it dug in 1853 to link the Royal Palace to the barracks in case of revolt. Never finished, it became a shelter during the bombings and later a police impound: the seized vintage cars and motorbikes are still there, covered in dust.
Evening: Piazza Bellini

A tree-lined square on top of Greek walls from the 4th century BC, which you can see in the open among the café tables. Students, bookshops, live music. It’s where Neapolitans have a drink before dinner, two minutes from Via dei Tribunali. For food, the polpette (meatballs) and pizza fritta (fried pizza) in the surrounding alleys are the best part.
Day 2: the upper city, the sea and the Sanità

Naples is a vertical city, and day two is for understanding that. The classic version is the Vomero in the morning and the sea in the afternoon. If you prefer neighbourhoods to views, the alternative is further down.
Morning: the Vomero, the Certosa di San Martino and Castel Sant’Elmo

Take the funicular up from Montesanto. San Martino is the highest point of the Vomero, where you see the whole city: the old centre with Spaccanapoli, the port, Vesuvius, and Capri on clear days. The Certosa, a former monastery, has the great cloister with marble skulls on the balustrade, the Baroque church and the collection of nativity scenes. Next door is Castel Sant’Elmo, a six-pointed star with an open terrace. If your legs are up to it, walk up or down the Pedamentina: 414 steps.
Afternoon: Chiaia, the seafront and Castel dell’Ovo

From the Vomero you go down to Chiaia by funicular, or on foot via the Petraio, the stairway that winds between Art Nouveau villas, vegetable gardens and glimpses of the bay you can’t see from the road. From Chiaia it’s a few minutes to the Lungomare Caracciolo, the seafront promenade, pedestrianised and flat all the way to Mergellina. At the end is Castel dell’Ovo, with the little harbour of Borgo Marinari at its feet. A bit further on is Piazza del Plebiscito: the colonnade of San Francesco di Paola on one side, the façade of the Palazzo Reale (the Royal Palace) on the other. You can cross it for free at any hour.
The alternative: Rione Sanità, the catacombs and the Fontanelle

The Sanità is the neighbourhood under the bridge that for decades Neapolitans themselves avoided. Start at the Catacombs of San Gennaro: two levels of galleries dug into the tuff from the 2nd century, with early Christian frescoes and the first tomb of the city’s patron saint. They’re run by a cooperative of young people from the neighbourhood, and it changed the area’s story. Then walk past Baroque palazzi to the Cimitero delle Fontanelle, a tuff quarry holding tens of thousands of skulls. For a century Neapolitans “adopted” a skull, one of the anime pezzentelle (the poor forsaken souls), asking for favours in return. It isn’t a macabre place: it’s quiet and cool.
Evening: Neapolitan song or a boat at sunset

Two evenings that beat the usual restaurant. The first is a concert of canzone napoletana, Neapolitan song, the way it used to be done: fifty-seat rooms in the centre, bare voices and mandolins, no amplification. The second, from May to October, is the bay from the water: small boats run along Posillipo at sunset, with seafront villas ahead and Vesuvius behind. If you’d rather not book anything, the seafront from Castel dell’Ovo to Mergellina is more than enough.
Day 3: out of town
On day three you leave the city, and there’s one rule: one trip only. Try to squeeze Pompeii and Capri into the same day and you’ll see neither. Here are the options, with their pros and cons.
Pompeii, in half a day

The obvious choice, and rightly so. But the site is big, shade is scarce and the streets are stone: on your own you walk a lot and understand little. It suits people who want to see the ruins and keep half a day for Naples. The [Pompeii tour with an archaeologist guide, ticket and coach from Naples](/esperienze/pompei-con-guida-archeologa-biglietto-e-pullman-da-napoli) lasts three and a half hours. If you want a whole day there on your own, take the Circumvesuviana, the local train that runs round Vesuvius.
Pompeii and Vesuvius, in one day

First the crater, then the city it buried. A coach takes you up to 1,000 metres, then there’s an uphill gravel path; at the top, the bay from Sorrento to Ischia. It suits people who want to do both without changing transport three times, and families with older kids. Two things to know about [Vesuvius and Pompeii in one day, with pizza on the slopes](/esperienze/vesuvio-e-pompei-in-un-giorno-con-pizza-sulle-pendici): the guide speaks English or Spanish, and in rain or strong wind the crater may be closed.
Herculaneum: smaller and more intact

Pompeii is more famous, Herculaneum is better preserved: the volcanic mud saved the upper floors of the houses, the charred furniture, the beams, the doors. You can see it in two hours, and it’s twenty minutes from Naples on the Circumvesuviana. It suits people who don’t like crowds and want the afternoon free. With [Herculaneum with an archaeologist, ticket included](/esperienze/ercolano-con-un-archeologo-biglietto-incluso), €35, the rooms become the homes of people with names.
Capri

Fifty minutes by hydrofoil. The island is as beautiful as they say, but it’s all slopes and steps, and in high season it’s crowded. It suits people who have always wanted to see it and can live with the crowds. The day on [Capri and Anacapri by hydrofoil, with the Gardens of Augustus](/esperienze/capri-e-anacapri-in-aliscafo-con-i-giardini-di-augusto) lasts eight hours, with the hydrofoil already booked, a minibus up to Anacapri and a guide. The Blue Grotto and Monte Solaro aren’t included.
Amalfi Coast

Let’s be honest: the Amalfi Coast deserves a trip of its own. On a day trip from Naples you get a taste, with plenty of hours of road and hairpin bends. It suits people who won’t be back this way soon and want to see the three towns without driving or hunting for parking. The [Sorrento, Positano and Amalfi by minibus, with photo stops](/esperienze/sorrento-positano-e-amalfi-in-minibus-con-soste-per-le-foto) tour gets back in the evening. If you get carsick, think twice.
Ischia and Procida

This isn’t a cultural outing, it’s a day at sea. It works in summer, for anyone who after two days of churches and museums just wants water; not for anyone prone to seasickness. With [Ischia and Procida by boat, with swims and lunch on board](/esperienze/ischia-e-procida-in-barca-con-bagni-e-pranzo-a-bordo) you take the hydrofoil from Molo Beverello, board a boat at Procida and sail along Ischia without landing. Seven hours in all.
Royal Palace of Caserta

The only trip that doesn’t look at the sea. The Reggia, the royal palace commissioned by Charles of Bourbon in 1750 and designed by Luigi Vanvitelli: 1,200 rooms and a park with three kilometres of avenues. A good pick when the weather is uncertain, and for anyone who loves palaces and gardens. You get there by train, and the palace is opposite Caserta station. The [Royal Palace of Caserta in three hours, with the grand staircase, the apartments and the park shuttle](/esperienze/reggia-di-caserta-in-tre-ore-scalone-appartamenti-e-navetta-al-parco) starts at the entrance: getting there is up to you.
Pick day three by checking the forecast. The islands and the coast lose half their charm with rough seas or rain; Pompeii, Herculaneum and Caserta work in almost any weather.
Where to stay to get around easily

items: Old centre: you do day one on foot and have Piazza Bellini on your doorstep in the evening. The trade-off is noise until late, scooters in the alleys and old buildings that don’t always have a lift.
Chiaia and the seafront: the most elegant area and the quietest at night, close to the sea and the hydrofoils. It costs more, and the old centre is half an hour’s walk away.
Vomero: residential and orderly, with San Martino within strolling distance. You come down by funicular and metro, but in the evening you depend on public transport.

Station area: the handiest for the Circumvesuviana, trains, the metro and day-trip coaches, and usually the cheapest. It’s chaotic and not very pleasant at night. Fine if you want to spend little and leave early.
napoli-in-3-giorni.content: With three days, the area matters more than the room. The four that make sense:
Getting around

Metro Line 1 is the one you need. It links the central station at Piazza Garibaldi with Università, Municipio, Toledo, Dante, Museo and Vanvitelli, up on the Vomero: practically every stop of the first two days. There are four funiculars. Three go up to the Vomero: the Centrale from Via Toledo, the Chiaia line, and the Montesanto line, the handiest for San Martino. The fourth climbs from Mergellina towards Posillipo.

For Pompeii and Herculaneum there’s the Circumvesuviana, on the Sorrento line. It leaves from Porta Nolana and stops at Piazza Garibaldi, under the central station. The stops you want are Ercolano Scavi and Pompei Scavi-Villa dei Misteri. The trains are basic and packed in high season: better to set off early. Hydrofoils to Capri, Ischia and Procida leave from Molo Beverello, opposite the Maschio Angioino castle, at the Municipio metro stop.
What to book before you go

Most of this itinerary needs no booking. A few things, though, left to the last minute, sell out or cost you a queue. Almost all our experiences can be cancelled free of charge up to 24 hours before, so booking them from home doesn’t tie your hands.

items: The Veiled Christ, above all. On your own, with a ticket bought in advance, or with the [Veiled Christ and Sansevero Chapel guided tour](/esperienze/cristo-velato-e-macchine-anatomiche-con-guida): 45 minutes with a licensed guide and ticket included, €15.
The day-three trip. In high season Capri and the Amalfi Coast fill up first.
[The MANN with an archaeologist](/esperienze/il-mann-con-unarcheologa-farnese-pompei-ed-ercolano): two hours, priority entry, €44. Money well spent, especially before Pompeii.
The [Galleria Borbonica: cisterns, shelters and vintage cars](/esperienze/galleria-borbonica-cisterne-rifugi-e-auto-depoca): one hour, €15. You can only go in on a guided tour.
[An hour of Neapolitan song, no microphones](/esperienze/unora-di-canzone-napoletana-senza-microfoni): €20 with a drink. Seats are few.
napoli-in-3-giorni.content: In order of urgency:
If you have two days, or four

With two days, keep day one as it is. Day two becomes a compromise: Pompeii or Herculaneum in the morning, San Martino and the seafront in the afternoon. The Sanità and the islands drop out, and so be it. If you only have one day, that’s a different itinerary and we’ve written it separately: [Naples in one day, hour by hour](/blog/napoli-in-un-giorno).

With four days, don’t add a second trip: add more Naples. A morning in the Quartieri Spagnoli and the Pignasecca, the city’s oldest street market. Then Capodimonte, with the Farnese collection, Caravaggio’s Flagellation, painted in Naples in 1607, and the Real Bosco, the royal park, all around. Or catch up on what you left out: the Sanità if you chose the sea, the MANN if you went underground.

One last thing. Naples changes every week: neighbourhood festivals, concerts, exhibitions, special openings. Before you leave, check [what’s on in Naples on your dates](/cosa-fare): we update the listings every morning.

cosa-fare-a-napoli-weekend-24-27-settemb.content: This is the weekend Naples looks out to sea: from Thursday 24 to Sunday 27 September the bay hosts the America’s Cup preliminary regattas, with Luna Rossa on the water and a free race village on the seafront. Around it: the Saturday of the European Heritage Days, with the Archaeological Museum open at night for €1, four nights of world music in a church in the old centre, three Sal Da Vinci concerts and a full day of electronic music in Bagnoli. Here’s everything day by day, with times, venues and prices checked at the source. The full listings are in [Things to do in Naples](/cosa-fare); the page that updates itself every morning is [this weekend](/cosa-fare/weekend).
Thursday to Sunday: the America’s Cup on the seafront

The Louis Vuitton Preliminary Regatta brings nine AC40s, the America’s Cup’s flying boats, into the bay, with Luna Rossa among the teams. Racing runs from the 25th to the 27th, every day from 2pm: eight fleet races and a two-boat final. The Race Village is at Rotonda Diaz on the Lungomare Caracciolo, the seafront promenade, open from 11am until evening, free to enter, with big screens to follow the racing. You only pay for what you eat or buy.

From the seafront you can see the boats well; from above, even better. The spots to head for are Via Petrarca, Via Orazio and Via Aniello Falcone, in Posillipo and the Vomero, where the whole race course opens up with Vesuvius behind. If you want to be on the water, you can watch from a boat: our [75-minute trip](/esperienze/il-golfo-in-75-minuti-vesuvio-castel-dellovo-posillipo-e-nisida) leaves from the port and runs right along that stretch, but on race days book early and ask about times.
Thursday 24 and Friday 25: Ethnos, the Certosa by night, Sal Da Vinci

From Thursday to Sunday the Ethnos Festival brings four nights of world music to the church of Santa Maria Donnalbina in the old centre: on the 24th Ensemble Enerbia and Maria Mazzotta, on the 25th ZeroFolkDuo and the Korean group Dal:um, on the 26th Constantinople with Ghalia Benali, on the 27th Raül Refree with Aida Tarrío. Concerts at 8.30pm and 9.30pm, on the 26th and 27th at 9pm; tickets €8–10. The best value for money of the week.

Friday 25 brings the second of the Notturni in Certosa at San Martino, evening visits to the former monastery with the city below: times and booking on the museum’s website. Friday is also the first of Sal Da Vinci’s three nights at the Arena Flegrea, marking fifty years since his debut, “Napoli, per sempre sì”: the 25th, 26th and 27th at 9pm, with the third date added after two sell-outs. Until Friday the tall ship Amerigo Vespucci is in port too, with free visits on board by booking only, via the tour’s official website.
Saturday 26: the MANN for €1 and the Heritage Days

For the European Heritage Days the National Archaeological Museum opens in the evening for a symbolic €1 ticket: 7pm–11.30pm, with music, dance and installations among the collections. If you’ve never seen the Pompeii mosaics and the Farnese Bull, this is your chance; if you have, at night they’re something else. If you’d rather understand them with someone who has studied them, there’s the [tour with an archaeologist](/esperienze/il-mann-con-unarcheologa-farnese-pompei-ed-ercolano) during normal opening hours.

At 6pm, free with compulsory booking, theatre comes to the Parco Vergiliano in Piedigrotta, among the tombs of Virgil and Leopardi, with “Progetto Cuccagna” from the Metamorfosi Campane season. On Saturday and Sunday at 10am the Tour del Giallo, a crime-story walk, stops at Piazza Mercato, among the murders of the war years: free, booking by email. And if you have kids, Saturday morning always means Giro Giro Napoli, free museum visits designed for them.

Out of town, at 6pm, “Calici e jazz di luna piena” (wine and full-moon jazz) among the vineyards of Somma Vesuviana: a walk in the vines, three wines, local dishes, live jazz and the moon through a telescope, €55.90 (€25.90 for non-drinkers and kids). And every Friday and Saturday until 10 October the Grande Pompei sites open at night, 7.30pm–11.30pm, €7 per site, while Biagio Antonacci plays an acoustic show at the Teatro Grande.
Sunday 27: Capriati in Bagnoli and the last Sunday in the park

From 2pm into the night, at the former NATO base in Bagnoli, Joseph Capriati celebrates twenty years of his career with a full day of electronic music and international guests; tickets online. At 2pm there’s also the last day of America’s Cup racing, with the final.

From 6pm to midnight, at the Parco del Poggio in Colli Aminei, the third and last Sunday of Social Park: DJ sets from BUSEX, ITALOMARIO and OKAMI, food, a market, a kids’ area and a dog area, and views over the city. Free entry with booking. It’s a series of evenings we’ve backed too: if you were there last Sunday, you already know what it’s like.
All weekend

items: OktoberDays at the Palapartenope, second weekend: Thursday to Sunday, long shared tables, Bavarian food, fairground rides and a kids’ area, tickets online
Pessoa Luna Park in the moat of Castel Sant’Elmo: Thursday to Sunday from 5.30pm, concerts, open-air cinema and shared tables, €2.50, until 4 October
Emilio Isgrò, “Canto Napoli” at Capodimonte: last few days, closes 29 September
Maria Lai at the Madre, the contemporary art museum, until 12 October, and Philip Colbert at Pompeii until 30 November
Vespero Napoletano, the city council’s slow-tourism festival: free walks and workshops in the neighbourhoods until 24 October
cosa-fare-a-napoli-weekend-24-27-settemb.content: Things running over several days:
If you’d rather book something certain

With the seafront packed for the regattas, the old centre is more pleasant than usual this weekend: the [street food tour](/esperienze/street-food-nel-centro-storico-con-una-guida-del-posto) and the [Galleria Borbonica](/esperienze/galleria-borbonica-cisterne-rifugi-e-auto-depoca) are ten minutes from the Race Village. If you want to get out of the city, the sea is still good: [Capri by hydrofoil](/esperienze/capri-e-anacapri-in-aliscafo-con-i-giardini-di-augusto) or [Ischia and Procida by boat](/esperienze/ischia-e-procida-in-barca-con-bagni-e-pranzo-a-bordo), with free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

For the regattas you don’t need to reach the Race Village early: you need to choose where to watch from. If you want the crowd and the big screens, Rotonda Diaz from 1pm. If you actually want to see the boats, go up to Via Petrarca on the Mergellina funicular and bring binoculars: the race course is right below you.

All the events, including the following week’s, are in [Things to do in Naples](/cosa-fare): pick your dates and see what’s on, with the experiences you can book on those days. Next month’s events are in [Naples events in October 2026](/blog/eventi-napoli-ottobre-2026).

cosa-fare-a-napoli-weekend-19-20-settemb.content: It’s the most Neapolitan weekend of the year: on Saturday 19 the city waits for the blood of San Gennaro, on Sunday 20 the tall ship Amerigo Vespucci sails into port, and in the evening you choose between a Cuban concert for €10, water lilies in bloom at the Mostra d’Oltremare and a Sunday in the park with us. Here’s everything day by day, with times, venues and prices, checked at the source. The full listings, beyond the weekend too, are on the [Things to do in Naples](/cosa-fare) page; the version that updates itself every morning is [this weekend](/cosa-fare/weekend).

A practical warning: on the 19th the old centre fills up from dawn and you can’t get near the Duomo after 9am. If the festival isn’t your thing, head for the sea or the hills that day and come back to the centre in the evening.
Saturday 19: San Gennaro at the Duomo

On 19 September Naples Cathedral celebrates the city’s patron saint, and the city waits for his blood to liquefy, as it has every year since the 15th century. The cathedral opens in the morning and fills up at once: if you want to see anything, arrive early; if you just want to soak up the day, wander Via Duomo and the decumani, the old centre’s ancient main streets, where the celebrations carry on outdoors until evening. Free, of course.

If you’d rather be by the sea, there’s the [Tour del Giallo in Posillipo](/cosa-fare/weekend): Saturday and Sunday at 10am from Calata dei Due Frati, a guided seaside walk through true crime and noir novels, free with booking by email. And if you have kids, every Saturday morning until December there’s Giro Giro Napoli, free visits to the city’s museums designed for them.
Saturday night: De Crescenzo, La Traviata in the courtyards, the Certosa by night

At 9pm Eduardo De Crescenzo brings “Essenze Jazz” to the Arena Flegrea on Viale Kennedy: the extra date added after June’s sell-out, tickets on etes.it. On Saturday and Sunday evening, meanwhile, “Traviata da Cortile” moves into the Kimbo courtyards: opera without the opera house, an arm’s length from the singers; details and booking from the organiser.

On Saturday and Sunday, from sunset, the moat of Castel Sant’Elmo hosts the Pessoa Luna Park: concerts, DJ sets, open-air cinema and shared tables, entry €2.50 (free for under-18s and over-65s), open Thursday to Sunday until 4 October. On Sunday evening the Notturni in Certosa return to San Martino too, evening visits with the city below: times and booking on the museum’s website.
Sunday 20: the Vespucci in port and a Bavarian festival

On Sunday the Amerigo Vespucci, the Italian Navy’s training ship, arrives in Naples and stays in port until the 25th. Visits on board are free but only with a named booking on the tour’s official website, which publishes the pier and times in the days before: no other channel issues passes, so be wary of anyone offering them.

At the Palapartenope on Via Barbagallo, Saturday and Sunday bring the first weekend of OktoberDays, the Bavarian festival with long shared tables, food, fairground rides and a kids’ area, tickets online. It’s on again from 24 to 27 September. At the Mostra d’Oltremare, until Sunday, there’s the international chess festival “Il Tesoro di San Gennaro”: if you play, sign up; if not, it’s still a nice place to watch people concentrating very hard.
Sunday evening: Eliades Ochoa, water lilies, Social Park

The best night of the weekend costs €10: at 9pm at Villa Vannucchi in San Giorgio a Cremano, Eliades Ochoa, the voice and guitar of the Buena Vista Social Club, plays for the Ethnos Festival. Twenty minutes from the centre on the Circumvesuviana, the local train that runs round Vesuvius, and a Vesuvian garden for Cuban son.

From 6pm, at the Mostra d’Oltremare, “Esedra in Fiore”: the water lilies in bloom in the monumental fountain at sunset, with an aerial dance performance over the water. Free with booking on Eventbrite, up to four places per person. At 7pm, free, the church of the SS. Annunziata hosts an evening of Piedigrotta Viva, songs and stories from the city’s oldest festival.

And then there’s our Sunday: 6pm to midnight at the Parco del Poggio in Colli Aminei, Social Park vol. II, with DJ sets, a live show from the Paradise City Breakers, food, a market, a kids’ area and a dog area, and views over the city from the park. Free entry with booking; it’s the event we sponsor, and you’ll find us there. The booking link is in the [weekend listings](/cosa-fare/weekend).
All weekend: exhibitions and festivals

items: Emilio Isgrò, “Canto Napoli” at Capodimonte: his erasures on the scores of Neapolitan songs, until 29 September, with the museum ticket
Maria Lai, “Essere è tessere” at the Madre, the contemporary art museum: until 12 October, €8
Philip Colbert at Pompeii, included in the site ticket, until 30 November
Evenings in the Grande Pompei: every Friday and Saturday until 10 October the Park’s sites open 7.30pm–11.30pm, €7 per site
Vespero Napoletano, the city council’s slow-tourism festival: walks and workshops in the neighbourhoods until 24 October, free while places last
cosa-fare-a-napoli-weekend-19-20-settemb.content: Things that carry on after Sunday:
If you’d rather book something certain

At weekends experiences sell out faster: the [75-minute boat trip round the bay](/esperienze/il-golfo-in-75-minuti-vesuvio-castel-dellovo-posillipo-e-nisida) is the easiest way to see the Vespucci from the water, the [street food tour in the old centre](/esperienze/street-food-nel-centro-storico-con-una-guida-del-posto) is the alternative to the San Gennaro crowds if you still want the decumani, and [Neapolitan song without microphones](/esperienze/unora-di-canzone-napoletana-senza-microfoni) rounds off a Sunday nicely. All with free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

On Saturday 19 the centre is packed from 8am: if you’re staying near the Duomo, head out early towards the sea and come back in the evening, when the festival is over and the pizzerias on Via dei Tribunali are reachable again. On Sunday the Circumvesuviana to San Giorgio a Cremano runs roughly every half hour: leave plenty of time for Eliades Ochoa.
The listings with all the events, including the following week’s, are in [Things to do in Naples](/cosa-fare): pick your dates and see what’s on, with the experiences you can book on those days.

quartieri-napoli-da-scoprire.content: Naples has many faces. The postcard one is beautiful and real, but it’s only the surface. To really understand the city you have to go into the neighbourhoods, the ones tourists don’t reach, the ones where Neapolitans live.

Chiaia is the elegant side of Naples, facing the sea and dotted with Art Nouveau palazzi, known here as liberty. Via dei Mille and Via Filangieri are the streets for quality shopping. But Chiaia is also the neighbourhood of historic cafés: the Gran Caffè Gambrinus is a short walk away, and Piazza dei Martiri is one of the most photogenic corners of the city.

The Rione Sanità had a rough reputation for decades. Today it’s one of the most interesting neighbourhoods in Naples: an experiment in social regeneration that turned the Catacombs of San Gennaro into one of the city’s most original cultural attractions. The murals on the buildings, the craft workshops, the market on Via Vergini: it all tells a story of rebirth.

Make time for the Catacombs of San Gennaro: run by a cooperative of young people from the neighbourhood, they offer a lively tour told by people who grew up there. One of the best visits in all of Naples.
3. Ponticelli: street art in a working-class district

Ponticelli is the outskirts in the truest sense of the word. Far from the tourist trail, this eastern part of Naples has become an open-air street art museum. The Parco dei Murales project brought artists from all over Italy and Europe to paint the council blocks, turning grey façades into works about memory, identity and redemption.

Antignano is a residential part of the Vomero, known above all for its local market, one of the liveliest in Naples. You’ll find everything here: Campanian fruit and veg, cheese, clothes, household goods. It’s everyday Naples, no filter.
5. Bagnoli: between the future and its industrial past

Bagnoli is a unique urban case in Italy. Where the Italsider steelworks once stood, employing generations of Neapolitans, there’s now a large regeneration project. The Città della Scienza science centre, the Coroglio coastline, the remains of industrial structures turned photo backdrops: Bagnoli is a neighbourhood suspended between industrial memory and the future.
Naples never ends. Every time you think you’ve seen it all, you turn into an alley and find yourself in a completely different world.

napoli-in-un-giorno.content: You can do Naples in one day, as long as you accept one thing: a day is enough to understand the city, not to see it. The old centre alone would need a week, and then there are the hills, the sea, the museums and everything that lies underground. Try to cram it all into twelve hours and you'll spend the day in taxis and see nothing.

The rule that works is simple: one area per time slot, and you get around on foot or by funicular. Morning in the old centre, pizza for lunch, afternoon in a museum or underground, late afternoon up on the Vomero hill, evening on the seafront. Distances are short, the climbs aren't: comfortable shoes and a light backpack. Below you'll find the hour-by-hour itinerary, then how to get around and what's worth booking before you go.
9am: breakfast with a sfogliatella, then the old centre

Start at Piazza del Gesù, with the diamond-point facade of the Gesù Nuovo church on one side and the spire of the Immacolata in the middle. Breakfast first, though: a warm sfogliatella, the ricotta-filled pastry, either riccia (crisp and flaky) or frolla (soft shortcrust), and a coffee standing at the bar, in a scalding cup. In Naples it often comes already sweetened, so ask for it amaro if you don't take sugar. Ten minutes and you're ready.

From the square, step into the cloister of Santa Chiara, where the pillars and benches are covered in 18th-century majolica tiles: it's the quietest spot of the whole morning. Then Spaccanapoli, the dead-straight street that splits the old centre in two and looks like a crack in the city when you see it from the Vomero. You walk it without a map, past San Domenico Maggiore, the workshops and the doorways open onto courtyards. Getting lost is part of the fun, but on a tight schedule keep your bearings: from Piazza del Gesù towards the Duomo, the cathedral.

The Cappella Sansevero is a stone's throw from San Domenico Maggiore. Inside is the Veiled Christ (Cristo Velato), carved by Giuseppe Sanmartino in 1753: a marble Christ under a veil that looks like fabric. You walk round the statue in silence, then go downstairs to see the anatomical machines, two skeletons with their circulatory systems on display. The chapel is small and crowded, and you need to buy your ticket in advance: without a booking the queue can eat your whole morning. If you'd also like someone to explain what you're looking at, there's [a 45-minute guided visit with the ticket included](/esperienze/cristo-velato-e-macchine-anatomiche-con-guida), €15.

Last stop of the morning: San Gregorio Armeno, the street of nativity scenes (presepi), where the workshops keep going all year and the figurines hang outside. From there you're on via dei Tribunali and, if you have time, the Duomo with the Chapel of the Treasure of San Gennaro is five minutes' walk away.
In the old centre you walk in the road, among the scooters. Keep to the right, don't stop in the middle of the lanes for photos, and wear your backpack closed and on your front.
1pm: pizza

At one o'clock you're between via dei Tribunali and via Duomo, which is exactly the right place. The pizzerias in the centre have a queue outside at any hour, and with only one day the queue is your enemy. Two ways round it: book a table in the morning for 1pm sharp, or get a pizza a portafoglio, folded in four and wrapped in paper, to eat as you walk. It costs a few euros and you're done in ten minutes. The margherita is the test of the oven; the marinara, with no mozzarella, the test of the dough. Skip the starters: Neapolitan pizza is big and the afternoon is long.
2.30pm: the MANN or underground

Here you have to choose, because you can't fit in both. Option one is the National Archaeological Museum, the MANN, ten minutes' walk from Piazza Bellini. Inside is the best of what the digs at Pompeii and Herculaneum have given back: the mosaics from the House of the Faun, the frescoes, the bronzes from the Villa of the Papyri, the Farnese Bull and the Farnese Hercules, the Secret Cabinet. It's a huge museum, and without a guide you come out tired, feeling you've missed the rooms that mattered. Two hours with an archaeologist is enough to leave with a clear picture.

Option two is going underground. Naples is dug into tuff, the soft volcanic stone, and beneath its streets lie cisterns, aqueducts and air-raid shelters. The Galleria Borbonica, under Chiaia, was dug on the orders of Ferdinand II in 1853 to link the Royal Palace to the barracks in case of revolt. It was never finished: in the 20th century it became an air-raid shelter, then a judicial impound, and the confiscated vintage cars and motorbikes are still down there today, covered in dust, next to the graffiti Neapolitans left during the bombing raids. You can only go in on a guided tour: [an hour in the Galleria Borbonica](/esperienze/galleria-borbonica-cisterne-rifugi-e-auto-depoca) costs €15. The alternative in the old centre is Napoli Sotterranea, with its entrance on via dei Tribunali and the aqueduct cisterns forty metres down.

How to choose: if you want to understand Pompeii without going there, the MANN. If it's hot, raining or you have children with you, underground. Either way, by 4.30pm you're out and a few minutes from a funicular.
5pm: up high

From the old centre you ride up to the Vomero on the Montesanto funicular; from Chiaia on the Chiaia one, from via Toledo on the Centrale. A few minutes and you're above the city without breaking a sweat. The highest point is Largo San Martino, home to the Certosa, the former Carthusian monastery, and Castel Sant'Elmo, a six-pointed star with an open terrace: from up there you see the whole city, the old centre with the crack of Spaccanapoli, the port, Vesuvius, and Capri on clear days.

The Certosa di San Martino has the great cloister with marble skulls on the balustrade, the Baroque church and the collection of nativity scenes, including the Cuciniello, the most famous of them. If you only have time for one thing, pick the castle. The San Martino belvedere, the terrace in front of the Certosa, is free and the right place for the six o'clock light.

To come down, the Neapolitan choice is the Pedamentina: 414 steps from the Certosa to corso Vittorio Emanuele, past vegetable gardens and glimpses of the bay you can't see from the road. From there it's half an hour's walk to the seafront, downhill all the way.
7.30pm: the seafront and Castel dell'Ovo

The lungomare, the seafront promenade from via Partenope to Mergellina, is traffic-free and flat, and at this hour it's full of Neapolitans strolling, jogging or sitting on the rocks. Castel dell'Ovo stands on a small island joined to the mainland, with the Borgo Marinari below it, a little harbour of boats and café tables. You can walk round the borgo in ten minutes and it's the right spot for sunset, with Vesuvius across the bay and Posillipo lighting up behind you.

For dinner you have three options: the trattorias of Santa Lucia and Chiaia, a short walk from the castle; a second pizza, which in Naples is no sin; or push dinner back to 9pm in the old centre, where the evening ends up anyway.
9pm: the evening

Two possible evenings, in opposite parts of town. Piazza Bellini sits on Greek walls from the 4th century BC, open to the sky among the café tables: students, bookshops, live music. It's where Neapolitans go for a drink, two minutes from via dei Tribunali, and in the lanes around it you'll find polpette (meatballs) and pizza fritta (fried pizza), which are the best part. Or Chiaia, the lanes between via dei Mille and Piazza dei Martiri, with tables outside and a smarter crowd. If you'd like something organised, the centre has concerts of Neapolitan song in fifty-seat rooms, an hour long after dinner and with no amplification: more on that below.
If you have a day and a half

With an extra half day, the next morning you either leave the city or head out on the water. The first option is Herculaneum (Ercolano): twenty minutes from Naples on the Circumvesuviana, the local railway that loops round Vesuvius. It's a small site you can cover in two hours, and more intact than Pompeii, because the volcanic mud preserved the upper floors of the houses, the charred furniture, the wooden beams, the doors. With an archaeologist the rooms turn into the homes of people with names: [the two-hour visit with ticket included](/esperienze/ercolano-con-un-archeologo-biglietto-incluso) costs €35. You're back in Naples for lunch.

The second option is seeing the bay from the sea. You leave from the port or the Borgo Marinari and follow the Posillipo coast: the villas, Palazzo Donn'Anna with its foundations in the water, the caves, the Gaiola, and behind you Vesuvius and the whole city. From May to October the small nine-seat boats stop for a swim; the rest of the year it's the classic 75-minute trip. It's the quickest way to understand the shape of the city.
Getting around

No car. The old centre is largely closed to traffic, parking is a job in itself and the traffic eats your hours. The whole itinerary works with three ways of getting around, and a single city ticket covers the metro, funiculars and buses.

items: On foot: from the old centre to the Museum, from via Toledo to Piazza del Plebiscito, from the Vomero down to the seafront. Distances are short, but the paving is basalt and the lanes climb: comfortable shoes, not new ones.

Metro Line 1: links Garibaldi station to the centre (Duomo, Università, Municipio, Toledo, Dante, Museo) and climbs to the Vomero, at the Vanvitelli stop. The Art Stations, Toledo above all, are worth a stop even if you're not going anywhere.
Funiculars: Montesanto, Centrale (from via Toledo) and Chiaia climb to the Vomero in a few minutes; the Mergellina line goes up to Posillipo.
Taxis: only for the airport or to get back to your hotel late at night. Ask for the fixed fare (tariffa predeterminata) before you set off.
napoli-in-un-giorno.content: In order of how much you'll use them:
What to book in advance

Four things, all bookable on our site, that fix the points where a single day gets wasted. The first is the Cappella Sansevero: the [Veiled Christ guided tour with the ticket included](/esperienze/cristo-velato-e-macchine-anatomiche-con-guida), 45 minutes, €15, from Piazza San Domenico Maggiore. It gets you past the queue that can eat the whole 9am section.

The second is [the MANN with an archaeologist](/esperienze/il-mann-con-unarcheologa-farnese-pompei-ed-ercolano), two hours with priority entry, €44: the Farnese collection, Pompeii and Herculaneum in the right order. It's the best money you'll spend all day.

The third is [the bay in 75 minutes](/esperienze/il-golfo-in-75-minuti-vesuvio-castel-dellovo-posillipo-e-nisida), €25 from the port, with live commentary and a covered deck: Vesuvius, Castel dell'Ovo, Posillipo and Nisida. It runs all year round, and if you have a day and a half it's your second morning.

The fourth is the evening: [an hour of Neapolitan song without microphones](/esperienze/unora-di-canzone-napoletana-senza-microfoni), €20 with a drink, in the Galleria Principe di Napoli, a short walk from the Museum. Bare voices and mandolins, the singers a metre away, and the stories behind each song told in between. It costs about as much as a pizza, and book ahead, because seats are few.

Buy your Cappella Sansevero ticket as soon as you know your date, not the night before. And almost all our experiences can be cancelled free of charge up to 24 hours before: if your plans change, you lose nothing.

Everything else, from the day's events to exhibitions, concerts and markets, is updated every morning on the [things to do in Naples](/cosa-fare) page. If your day falls on a Saturday or Sunday, check the listings: there may be a neighbourhood festival or a special opening worth a detour.

halloween-a-napoli-2026.content: This year Halloween falls on a Saturday and All Saints' Day (Ognissanti) on a Sunday, so you get a full long weekend, and Monday 2 November is the Day of the Dead. Halloween reached Naples late and settled on top of something much older: a city that talks to its dead, adopts them and brings them sweets. To spend 31 October here you don't need a costume. You need a sweatshirt, because you'll be going underground, and a couple of bookings made in good time.

Below are the places where this story really shows, with opening times taken from the official sites. Most of the 2026 themed events are announced in mid-October: where you need to check, we'll say so.
Saturday 31 October: under the city, even after dark

The underground is the most sensible place to spend Halloween in Naples, because down there the fear isn't fake: Greek quarries, cisterns, shelters where people slept through the bombs. Napoli Sotterranea starts from Piazza San Gaetano 69, on via dei Tribunali, with tours in Italian and English every hour, 10am–6pm. You go down among the Greco-Roman aqueduct and the wartime shelters. The evening tour runs only on Thursdays at 9pm, by booking and with at least ten people: if you arrive on Thursday 29, give it a try.

On the other side of the centre is the [Galleria Borbonica](/esperienze/galleria-borbonica-cisterne-rifugi-e-auto-depoca), the tunnel the king had dug under Chiaia: cisterns, air-raid shelters and vintage cars and motorbikes left down there since the war. In recent years, on 30 and 31 October, the Galleria has run a Halloween night on rafts across the underground water table, with evening slots and places that go fast. For 2026 it hasn't been announced yet: keep an eye on their website from early October. The regular tours run as usual in the meantime.

Tours with actors in the lanes and parties in bars change every year and are announced in the two weeks before. The place to gather is still Piazza Bellini, which is packed on a Saturday night anyway.

Local tip: on the evening of the 31st the old centre fills up with young people in costume, and the bars around Piazza Bellini are rammed by midnight. If you want a sit-down dinner, book, or eat early by Neapolitan standards: that means by 8.30pm.
The Fontanelle and the anime pezzentelle

If one place explains why Halloween in Naples isn't an imported holiday, it's the Cimitero delle Fontanelle, at via Fontanelle 80, in the Rione Sanità neighbourhood. It's a tuff quarry of about 3,000 square metres where, for centuries, the bones of epidemic victims and of the poor with no grave ended up. This is where the cult of the anime pezzentelle, the "poor souls", was born: a family would choose a nameless skull, clean it, build it a little house of wood or marble and pray to it. In return the soul, from purgatory, was meant to send a favour, sometimes a dream with the lottery numbers.

Since 18 April 2026 the cemetery has been open again on a permanent basis, run by the La Paranza cooperative together with the city council. It's open 10am–6pm, last entry 5.15pm, closed on Wednesdays, and online booking is always required. It's open on Saturday 31 and Sunday 1; on Mondays and Fridays there's also an hour, 9am–10am, that's free and reserved for prayer only. On Monday 2 November, the Day of the Dead, that hour shows you the cult as it still lives today.
Local tip: over the long weekend the Fontanelle slots go weeks ahead. Book as soon as you have your dates, then build the rest of the day around that time: the Sanità is easy to explore on foot.
Sunday 1 November: the catacombs of San Gennaro and San Gaudioso

A quarter of an hour's walk from the Fontanelle are the Catacombs of San Gennaro, two levels of underground basilicas with frescoes more than a thousand years old and the mosaics of the Crypt of the Bishops, and the Catacombs of San Gaudioso, beneath the Basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità. At San Gaudioso, in the 17th century, nobles had themselves buried with their skull set into the wall and their body painted below it: it's the closest thing to a Halloween image you'll find in a church.

One ticket covers both catacombs and the basilica. Watch the holiday opening hours: San Gennaro opens only 10am–1pm on Sundays and public holidays, San Gaudioso every day 10am–5pm. So on Sunday 1 start with San Gennaro in the morning and leave San Gaudioso for the afternoon. Here you'll find [the guided tour of the Catacombs of San Gennaro](/esperienze/sotto-la-sanita-le-catacombe-di-san-gennaro), in Italian or English.
Munaciello and bella 'mbriana: the other tenants

Every Neapolitan home, they say, has two tenants who don't pay rent. The bella 'mbriana is the good spirit, an elegant lady who protects whoever lives there: you greet her when you come in. The munaciello is more complicated. He's a little monk who moves things around, makes your keys vanish and now and then leaves a coin. Matilde Serao, in her Leggende napoletane (Neapolitan Legends), has him born of a 15th-century love affair that ended badly; the more down-to-earth explanation links him to the pozzari, the men who cleaned the cisterns and could climb into houses at night through the wells. If you go down into Napoli Sotterranea, you'll see those wells.

Legends are best told on foot. On via dei Tribunali stands the church of Purgatorio ad Arco, with bronze skulls on the facade and, underneath, the hypogeum where people venerate the skull of Lucia, wearing a bridal veil. It's one of the stops on the walk [origins, cults and legends of the old centre with an archaeologist](/esperienze/origini-culti-e-leggende-del-centro-storico-con-un-archeologo), two and a half hours from the Greek walls to the Duomo.
Monday 2 November: the dead and the torrone

On 2 November Naples goes to the cemetery at Poggioreale, among flowers and chatter. At home a sweet appears that exists only in these days: torrone dei morti, 'o murticiello. It has nothing to do with Christmas nougat. It's soft, made of chocolate with hazelnuts, and often shaped like a little coffin: the tavùto. Tradition says the dead come back on the night between the 1st and the 2nd, and the sweet is there to sweeten their journey.

From late October, pastry shop windows fill up with torroncini in dozens of flavours, from classic to pistachio, gianduia and coffee, sold whole or by the slice. Ask for the soft chocolate one with hazelnuts: that's the traditional one.
Local tip: torrone dei morti is meant to be given. If you're a guest in someone's home over the long weekend, bringing one counts for more than a bottle of wine.

For the long weekend, the version that works: Saturday 31 underground by day and the old centre at night, Sunday 1 the Sanità with its catacombs and the Fontanelle, Monday 2 a torrone and a walk around town. On the [map of Naples](/mappa) you can see how close these places are: from the Sanità to Piazza San Gaetano is barely half an hour on foot. Halloween events, as they're announced, go into [things to do in Naples](/cosa-fare), with the long weekend's dates and the experiences you can book on those days.

costiera-amalfitana-da-napoli.content: You can do the Amalfi Coast from Naples in a day, as long as you accept two things: you'll spend half of it on buses, trains or boats, and you'll see two towns, not six. Positano, Amalfi and Ravello are only a few kilometres apart, but on a road of hairpin bends where a bus crawls along at thirty kilometres an hour. Here are the two ways to get there without a car, what to choose if you only have one day, and why you're better off leaving the car behind.
By train and bus: Circumvesuviana to Sorrento, then SITA

This is the option that works all year. From Naples take the Circumvesuviana, the local railway run by EAV, on the Napoli–Sorrento line, from Porta Nolana or from the Piazza Garibaldi station: it takes about an hour and a quarter to Sorrento, with plenty of stops on the way. In summer there was also the Campania Express, the tourist train with few stops, but EAV suspended it from 1 October 2026 until further notice: in autumn you travel on the ordinary trains.

The blue SITA Sud buses to the coast leave from outside Sorrento station. The Amalfi line goes through Positano: you reach Positano in about forty minutes and Amalfi in a good hour and a half, longer in traffic. For Ravello, change at Amalfi and ride up on another SITA bus, half an hour of hairpins. Buy your ticket beforehand, at a tabaccheria (tobacconist), a bar or a newsstand, on the Unico Costiera fares; if you're taking more than two rides, the day ticket is the better deal.

Local tip: on the bus from Sorrento to Positano, sit on the right-hand side. The sea is all on that side, and the hairpin above Positano, where the town suddenly appears below you, is the photo of the day.
By sea: hydrofoils from Molo Beverello, until early November

From spring to autumn you can also reach Positano and Amalfi by hydrofoil from Molo Beverello, the main ferry pier in Naples, with NLG, Alilauro and other operators. NLG's 2026 timetable on the Naples–Amalfi route runs from 1 April to 3 November, with fewer sailings in the last few weeks; some departures involve a change at Capri or Sorrento. The crossing takes an hour and a half or more, depending on the stops: it's no faster than train plus bus, but you arrive from the sea, which for Positano and Amalfi is the right way in.

Between the towns on the coast, from April to October, there are also Travelmar's local ferries linking Salerno, Amalfi and Positano. For a day trip from Naples the handiest combination is often this: bus to Positano, ferry from Positano to Amalfi, and back from Amalfi by hydrofoil or bus.

Local tip: in October the sea decides. With a southerly wind, hydrofoils and coastal ferries can be cancelled on the morning itself. Always keep plan B, the SITA bus, up your sleeve, along with the time of the last train from Sorrento.
Positano, Amalfi, Ravello and the Path of the Gods

Positano is the vertical town: the houses tumble down to the Spiaggia Grande, the main beach, and you do everything on foot, by staircase. The route is simple: from the bus stop at the top, walk down via Cristoforo Colombo and via dei Mulini to the church of Santa Maria Assunta with its majolica dome, then the sea. Then comes the climb back up, which some people remember more than the view.

Amalfi was once a maritime republic and it shows: the Duomo di Sant'Andrea at the top of a flight of about sixty steps, the Cloister of Paradise next door, the old paper mills in the Valle dei Mulini. Ravello sits three hundred metres higher, with Villa Rufolo and Villa Cimbrone, and the Terrace of Infinity looking along the whole coast towards Salerno. It's the quietest of the three, even in summer.

The Sentiero degli Dei, the Path of the Gods, is the coast seen from above. It starts in Bomerano, a village that is part of Agerola, and ends in Nocelle, above Positano: about eight kilometres, three or four hours' walking without big climbs but with stretches along sheer drops. You get to Bomerano on the SITA bus from Amalfi, about forty minutes; from Nocelle you go down to Positano by a long flight of steps or on the local bus. You'll need hiking shoes, water and a day with clear skies.
Traffic, odd-even number plates and why to leave the car

The SS163 Amalfitana is one of the most beautiful roads in Italy, and also a forty-kilometre queue. From 1 June to 31 October 2026 an order from ANAS, the state road agency, restricts non-residents to alternate days by number plate between Vietri sul Mare and Positano, 10am–6pm: every day in August and September, and only on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays in October. On odd dates, cars with plates ending in an odd number can drive; on even dates, the rest. Motorbikes and scooters are exempt.

Even when your plate is right, there's still parking: in Positano and Amalfi spaces are few and expensive, and the centres are pedestrian or limited-traffic zones. For a single day, the bus, the boat or an organised tour will save you time and nerves.
One day only: which to choose

items: First time, and you want the postcard: Positano in the morning, ferry to Amalfi, afternoon between the Duomo and the lanes, back by hydrofoil while the sailings last.
If you like walking: the Path of the Gods from Bomerano to Nocelle, down to Positano and the bus to Sorrento. Start early.
If you're after some calm: Amalfi and Ravello, with lunch up high and sunset from the Terrace of Infinity.
If you don't want to think about anything: an organised day from Naples, with transport waiting for you.

costiera-amalfitana-da-napoli.content: For that last option there are several formats. [Sorrento, Positano and Amalfi by minibus](/esperienze/sorrento-positano-e-amalfi-in-minibus-con-soste-per-le-foto) covers all three towns in a small group, with photo stops. [Positano and Amalfi by coach, with the ferry between the two](/esperienze/positano-e-amalfi-in-pullman-con-traghetto-tra-i-due-paesi) gives you three hours in Positano and two in Amalfi, and from April to October the stretch in between is done by boat. [Amalfi and Ravello from Naples](/esperienze/amalfi-e-ravello-da-napoli-con-assaggio-di-limoncello) sticks to two towns instead of three, with free time to explore them.

If the coast is one stop on a longer trip, read our guide to [Pompeii from Naples](/blog/pompei-da-napoli-come-arrivare) too: the ruins are on the same Circumvesuviana line, and some people fit them into the same day, with a very early alarm. You'll find other trips out of town in the [Outdoor](/categoria/outdoor) section, and the departure points on the [map of Naples](/mappa).

mostre-a-napoli-settembre-2026-da-vedere.content: September is the month when the summer exhibitions in Naples close and the autumn ones haven't opened yet. This week the lights went out on OBEY at the Gallerie d'Italia and on Carlo Maria Mariani at Capodimonte, both of which ended on 6 September. Four are left that are worth the ticket, plus one you can put off without feeling guilty.

Isgrò is the artist of erasures: he takes a text and blacks out almost every word, leaving visible only the ones that count. For Capodimonte he worked on twenty-five scores of Neapolitan songs. The result is a kind of silent score that anyone who knows the songs can still sing. The Museo e Real Bosco di Capodimonte is open 8.30am–7.30pm, closed on Wednesdays; the exhibition is included in the museum ticket.
2. Maria Lai, “Essere è tessere”, Madre (until 12 October)

Sixty years' work by a Sardinian artist who used thread, fabric and sewn books to talk about memory and community. It's the most complete retrospective in town, at the Museo Madre, the contemporary art museum on via Settembrini, alongside two other exhibitions that close on 5 October: “Gli anni. Capitolo 3” and “Living Collapse”. Hours: 10am–7.30pm Monday to Saturday, until 8pm on Sundays, closed on Tuesdays. Tickets €8 full price, €4 reduced.
3. “Il colore di Mimmo Jodice”, Museo del Tesoro di San Gennaro (until 10 January 2027)

Jodice is the photographer who told the story of Naples in black and white for half a century. This exhibition shows the other half of his archive, the colour half, inside the museum next to the Duomo. It's the one you can put off, but 19 September, the feast of San Gennaro, is the best day to go: you'll be there anyway.

Colbert's pop lobsters, planted among the Roman houses of the Archaeological Park of Pompeii. They divide opinion: some find them brilliant, others out of place. Either way the show is included in the ticket to the ruins, so forming your verdict costs nothing.

It isn't an exhibition, but if you like looking at art without the crowds it beats most exhibitions. The National Archaeological Museum opens in the evening, 7pm–11.30pm, on Thu 17 September and then on 1, 8, 15 and 22 October; tickets €10. On Sat 26 September, for the European Heritage Days, it costs €1.

When you leave the Madre, turn right onto via Duomo and walk 300 metres to the Pio Monte della Misericordia. Above the altar hangs Caravaggio's “The Seven Works of Mercy” (“Le Sette Opere della Misericordia”), from 1607. No temporary exhibition beats that painting.
If you'd like to see art with someone who explains it, the Art section has guided tours of Capodimonte, the catacombs and the Cappella Sansevero, with places you can book.

cosa-fare-a-napoli-quando-piove.content: It doesn't rain often in Naples, but when it does, it means it: half an hour of water pouring down the alleys like a river, and then the sun often comes back out. Planning your day around the forecast is pointless. What makes sense is having a list of indoor things ready to pull out the moment the sky closes in.

The good news is that Naples has a second city beneath and inside the first: tufa tunnels, cisterns, catacombs, air-raid shelters, churches, covered arcades, huge museums. Almost everything worth seeing doesn't depend on the weather. Below are ideas grouped by type, with duration and price for the activities you can book with us, plus a list of things to skip.
Underground: the Naples that stays dry

The Galleria Borbonica (Bourbon Tunnel), beneath Chiaia, is the place to start. Ferdinand II had it dug in 1853 to link the Royal Palace to the barracks in case of revolt. It was never finished: it became an air-raid shelter, then a police impound, and the seized vintage cars and motorbikes are still down there, covered in dust, next to the writing Neapolitans left on the walls during the bombings. An hour underground that tells you more about the city than plenty of museums. Guided tours only.

Napoli Sotterranea is the other classic descent: forty metres down, into the tufa quarries the Greeks opened to build the city, later used as an aqueduct and, during the war, as a shelter. In places you squeeze through narrow passages by candlelight, so if tight spaces bother you, know that before you go. This one is also guided and lasts about an hour.

In the Rione Sanità, below the Capodimonte hill, are the Catacombs of San Gennaro: two levels of galleries dug into the tufa from the 2nd century, with early Christian frescoes and the first tomb of the city's patron saint. They're run by a cooperative of young people from the neighbourhood. The ticket also covers the Catacombs of San Gaudioso, under the Basilica della Sanità: one ticket fills a morning, and the two are a few minutes' walk apart, umbrella in hand.

Also in the Sanità, at the far end of the neighbourhood, is the Cimitero delle Fontanelle: a tufa quarry holding tens of thousands of skulls and bones, piled up after the plagues and the 19th-century cholera. For a century Neapolitans 'adopted' a skull, one of the anime pezzentelle (the poor, forgotten souls), asking for favours in return; the Church banned the cult in 1969, but you still see lottery tickets tucked next to the skulls. It isn't macabre: it's quiet and cool.
The right museums for a rainy day

The Museo Archeologico Nazionale (MANN) is where three hours go by without you noticing: the mosaics from the House of the Faun, the frescoes from Pompeii, the bronzes from the Villa of the Papyri, the Farnese Bull and the Farnese Hercules. It's enormous, and on your own you tend to leave tired, with the feeling you missed the best bits. Of the [guided museum visits](/categoria/arte) we offer, the MANN with an archaeologist is the one that pays off most: two hours and you come out knowing what you've seen.

The Cappella Sansevero, with Giuseppe Sanmartino's Veiled Christ (1753) and the anatomical machines in the crypt, is small and very crowded. In the rain the problem is the queue outside: book your ticket in advance, or you'll spend half the afternoon getting wet on the pavement. You're inside for about half an hour, so pair it with something else nearby.

Capodimonte is the choice if you have a whole day. The palace on the hill houses the Farnese collection: Titian, Raphael, Masaccio, the Bruegels, and Caravaggio's Flagellation, painted in Naples in 1607. It's big and a long way from the centre: leave the Real Bosco (the royal park) for another time and spend half a day inside.

The Certosa di San Martino, up in the Vomero, is reached by funicular from Montesanto, so you're under cover almost all the way. The viewpoint is useless with low cloud, but the Certosa is the best part anyway: the great cloister with marble skulls on the balustrade, the baroque church, the nativity scenes including the Cuciniello crib. Castel Sant'Elmo next door has an open terrace: save it for a sunny day.
Hands-on: pizza and pasta

A pizza workshop takes two or three hours, indoors, and ends at the table with what you've made. Dough from flour, water, salt and very little yeast, stretched by hand with no rolling pin, then sixty seconds in a 450°C oven: you take the stretching technique home with you, along with the tiramisù made in the meantime. It's the most booked experience in Naples, and when it rains it's the first to sell out.

Fresh pasta is the alternative: ravioli, fettuccine, gnocchi, flour and eggs on the table, two sauces, a glass of wine, and at the end everyone eats together. The €20 versions are among the cheapest and most successful things in the city. In the [workshops](/categoria/laboratori) section you'll find every variation, with duration and price; some even include luggage storage, handy on departure day when it's raining and your suitcase is a problem.
Covered arcades and passages

Naples has two 19th-century arcades where you can stay dry for free. The Galleria Umberto I, between Via Toledo and the Teatro San Carlo, has a glass-and-iron dome and the signs of the zodiac on the floor: you can walk through it in five minutes, but in the rain it's where Neapolitans wait for it to stop. The Galleria Principe di Napoli, opposite the Archaeological Museum, is smaller and quieter, and in the evening hosts concerts of Neapolitan song with no microphones: an hour after dinner, for the price of a pizza.

Then there are the 'art stations' of metro line 1. Toledo, with its light well and blue mosaics, is the most famous, but you can do the whole tour without going outside: get off at Toledo, pass through Università and Municipio, and come up at Museo for the MANN. A museum spread across the city, under cover, for the price of a metro ticket.
Eating for hours

A tasting tour of the historic centre lasts two and a half hours: six or seven stops at the right shops for pizza a portafoglio (a small pizza folded in four and eaten on the go), frittatina di pasta (a fried pasta patty), pizza fritta, sfogliatella (the shell-shaped pastry filled with ricotta and semolina) and babà. You walk a few minutes between stops and spend the rest of the time at the counter. Go on an empty stomach and don't book dinner. The options are in the [food](/categoria/food) section.

If you just want to sit down, go for lunch at a winery on the slopes of Vesuvius: minibus from Naples, a walk among the Lacryma Christi vines, then a meal of what the estate produces. It's four hours and most of it is spent at the table. If you're staying in the centre, there's the classic Neapolitan way to kill time: a warm sfogliatella and a coffee standing at the bar, while you wait for it to pass.
With children in the rain

With younger kids, anything where they get to do something works. The pizza workshop is the obvious choice: they get their hands dirty, eat what they've made, and three hours fly by. The Galleria Borbonica, with its vintage cars in the dust, wins over even those with zero interest in the Bourbons. The underground sites are fine for kids who aren't afraid of the dark; for the Fontanelle, judge by their age. At the MANN the mosaics hold their attention better than you'd think, but go with a guide. Our [family guide](/blog/cosa-fare-a-napoli-con-i-bambini) has more ideas, with duration and group size.
What to avoid when it rains

items: Viewpoints: San Martino, Castel Sant'Elmo, Posillipo. With low cloud you can't see the bay, and the view was the only reason to go up.
Vesuvius: the path to the crater is gravel, it's windy at the top, and with cloud on the rim you see nothing. In bad weather organised trips can be cancelled.
Boats: trips round the bay are cancelled when the sea is rough, and anyway the whole point was the sun on Posillipo.
Walking Spaccanapoli: the alleys flood quickly and the wet basoli (the old lava paving stones) are slippery. If you must, hop in and out of the churches.
The Petraio and Pedamentina steps: 414 wet steps are no stroll.
Cycling: the pedestrian seafront with the rain coming in sideways is nobody's idea of fun.
cosa-fare-a-napoli-quando-piove.content: These are things you do in Naples when the sun's out; in the rain they're time wasted:

Almost all our experiences can be cancelled free of charge up to 24 hours before. Book the boat or Vesuvius for tomorrow and, if the forecast gets worse the evening before, switch to the Galleria Borbonica. When it rains, the indoor places sell out first.
What to book for a rainy day
Five things from our catalogue that don't care about the weather, with duration and price per person.

[Galleria Borbonica: cisterns, shelters and vintage cars](/esperienze/galleria-borbonica-cisterne-rifugi-e-auto-depoca), 1 hour, €15. Groups of up to eight, guide in Italian or English. The cheapest and most rewarding thing on this list.

[The MANN with an archaeologist: Farnese, Pompeii and Herculaneum](/esperienze/il-mann-con-unarcheologa-farnese-pompei-ed-ercolano), 2 hours, €44. Priority entry and an archaeologist: the two hours in which the city's biggest museum stops being a maze.

[Catacombs of San Gaudioso, beneath the Basilica della Sanità](/esperienze/catacombe-di-san-gaudioso-sotto-la-basilica-della-sanita), 45 minutes, €13. Guide and entry; the ticket also covers San Gennaro, so you get the whole of the Sanità.

[Pizza nel ruoto and tiramisù, the way it's made at home](/esperienze/pizza-nel-ruoto-e-tiramisu-come-si-fa-a-casa), 2½ hours, €30. Pizza nel ruoto is baked in a round tin, as Neapolitans do at home. Groups of up to fifteen, recipe booklet and luggage storage: the one to pick if it rains on the day you leave.

[Fresh pasta and tiramisù with a welcome glass, for €20](/esperienze/pasta-fresca-e-tiramisu-con-calice-di-benvenuto-a-venti-euro), 3 hours, €20. Prosecco, a starter, a diploma at the end and three hours under cover: the best ratio of time filled to money spent.
If it's raining today

Our [things to do in Naples today](/cosa-fare/oggi) page is updated every morning: exhibitions, concerts, special openings, with times, venue and price checked at the source. In the rain it's the most useful page we have: there's almost always a hall, a theatre or a museum on the listings where you can wait it out.
If a storm catches you in an alley in the centre, don't run for the metro: duck into the first open church or bar, have a coffee and wait. After twenty minutes it has almost always stopped.

campi-flegrei-cosa-vedere-in-un-giorno.content: The Campi Flegrei (Phlegraean Fields) are the part of Naples tourists skip: a volcano twelve kilometres wide with lakes, Roman baths, a Greek city older than Rome and a stretch of coast where emperors' villas lie underwater. From Montesanto it's half an hour by train. Below is a one-day route by public transport, covering what's open right now.

One thing before you go. On 31 July 2026 the area had its strongest earthquake in forty years. The Archaeological Park sites reopened after safety checks, and the Cumana railway has been running the full line again since 11 September. The Rione Terra in Pozzuoli, however, is closed, and rooms or routes can change from one week to the next: check the Info page on pafleg.cultura.gov.it the evening before and you're sorted.
Getting there and what to buy beforehand

The train is the Cumana, an EAV line from Montesanto to Torregaveta, running roughly every twenty minutes. The stops you need are Pozzuoli, Lucrino, Baia and Fusaro. Cuma has no station below the acropolis: from Fusaro it's a few kilometres by bus or taxi, and it's worth deciding which beforehand.

The ticket to get is the CircuitoFlegreo: €10, valid for three days, covering four sites: the Anfiteatro Flavio, the Museum in the Castle of Baia, the Baia Baths and Cuma. It's €5 for EU citizens aged 18 to 25, free under 18. Since April 2026 the ticket offices have been closed: you can only buy online, on the Musei Italiani website or app, booking a time slot. Entry is capped at 50 people every half hour, 25 at the amphitheatre.

Local tip: pick your day carefully. The Baia museum and baths close on Mondays, the amphitheatre and Cuma on Tuesdays. From Wednesday to Sunday you can do everything; on Wednesdays and at weekends the Piscina Mirabilis opens too.
Morning: Pozzuoli, the amphitheatre and the temple that rises and sinks

Get off at Pozzuoli and you've already started. The Anfiteatro Flavio is five minutes from the station, opens at 9am and is the third largest in Italy, after the Colosseum and the one at Capua. The highlight is underground: the corridors where the wild animals' cages stood and the lifts that hoisted them up into the arena. Access to the underground section often changes after tremors, so when you book, check what your time slot includes. You get thirty minutes, and that's enough.

Then head down towards the harbour, ten minutes on foot, and look over the Macellum, which everyone calls the Temple of Serapis. It was the market of Roman Puteoli. The three marble columns have a pitted band halfway up: holes bored by marine molluscs, proof that the ground here sank below sea level and then rose again. It's bradyseism (the slow rise and fall of the ground) explained without words. The site is closed, but you can see everything from the low wall on the square.
Lunch and early afternoon: Baia, the castle and the underwater villas

Two stops on the Cumana and you're in Baia, where wealthy Romans came for the baths and the parties. The Aragonese castle above the harbour houses the Archaeological Museum of the Campi Flegrei, open 9am–6.30pm with last entry at 5.30pm: inside is the Nymphaeum of Punta Epitaffio, rebuilt with the statues raised from the seabed, which explains what you're about to see in the water.

The Parco delle Terme di Baia (Baia Baths) is a kilometre uphill, open Tuesday to Sunday: terraces stepping down to the sea with pools, nymphaea, stucco work and the so-called Temple of Mercury, a round hall with a Roman concrete dome older than the Pantheon. Allow an hour and a half and wear shoes with decent soles.

The bit you won't find anywhere else is underwater. The villas and streets of Roman Baia lie a few metres down in front of the harbour, in the Parco Sommerso (Underwater Park): mosaics, columns, and statues put back where the originals stood. You can see it from a glass-bottomed boat, about an hour without getting wet, or with mask and fins. [Snorkelling over the sunken Roman villas of Baia](/esperienze/snorkeling-sulle-ville-romane-sommerse-di-baia) leaves from the harbour in groups of eight at most: two and a half hours with a guide and gear, €35. In September and early October the water is still good; you need a calm sea, otherwise you won't see much.

For lunch, between Baia harbour and Bacoli nearly every place does fish and nearly every place looks out over the water. A plate of fried fish or pasta with mussels, and a glass of Falanghina, the local white wine that calls this area home.
Afternoon: Cuma and the Cave of the Sibyl

Cuma (ancient Cumae) is the oldest Greek colony in the West, founded in the second half of the 8th century BC. The archaeological park sits on a tufa acropolis overlooking the sea, with the temples of Apollo and Jupiter. The Antro della Sibilla (Cave of the Sibyl) is a trapezoidal gallery cut into the tufa, more than a hundred metres long, with openings that slice the light into strips. Whether Virgil's prophetess really lived there is another matter, but once you're inside you stop wondering. Access is limited to 25 people at a time, visits last two hours at most, and it's closed on Tuesdays.

If you'd rather stay close to the railway, the alternative is the Piscina Mirabilis in Bacoli: the cistern of the Roman fleet at Misenum, an underground hall of pillared aisles that looks like a cathedral. It opens on Wednesdays, Saturdays and Sundays, visits are accompanied and start every half hour, it costs €5 and booking is compulsory.
Sunset: Lake Averno or Capo Miseno

To finish you have two options, both free. The first is Lake Averno, a crater full of water that the Romans considered the gateway to the underworld: it's where Virgil sends Aeneas down. From Lucrino station it's a quarter of an hour on foot, and the loop round the lake is a flat walk of just over an hour among vineyards and reed beds. At sunset it's the quietest place in the Campi Flegrei.

The second is Capo Miseno, at the tip of the peninsula: the beaches of Miseno and Miliscola face Procida, a stone's throw away, and at the end of September you can still swim if it's sunny. From Baia it's a few kilometres by bus or taxi; to get back to Naples, pick up the Cumana at Torregaveta, the end of the line, or at Fusaro.

Local tip: don't try to do everything. The version that works is Pozzuoli in the morning, Baia at lunchtime with the castle and the underwater villas, then just one of Cuma, the Piscina Mirabilis and Lake Averno. Save the rest for next time: the ticket lasts three days anyway.
If the sea calls louder than history

The Campi Flegrei are the right trip if you've already done Pompeii and want somewhere Neapolitans actually go. If one of your [three days in Naples](/blog/napoli-in-3-giorni) is still free, this is the answer. If Baia has left you wanting nothing but water, from the centre there's a boat out to [snorkelling in the Roman grottoes of Posillipo with a marine biologist](/esperienze/grotte-romane-e-fondali-di-posillipo-con-una-biologa-marina), and from Procida a [boat day around Ischia and Procida with lunch on board](/esperienze/ischia-e-procida-in-barca-con-bagni-e-pranzo-a-bordo).

Other day trips and boat outings are in the [Outdoor](/categoria/outdoor) section. And before you pick your day, check [what's on in Naples](/cosa-fare) that week: the Campi Flegrei often have an evening opening or a concert among the ruins.

reggia-di-caserta-da-napoli.content: The Reggia di Caserta (Royal Palace of Caserta) is the easiest day trip you can take from Naples: one regional train, five minutes on foot and you're in front of the palace. The hard part comes later, because inside there are more than a thousand rooms and a park three kilometres long. Here's how to get there, which ticket to buy, what to see and how to avoid spending half the day walking past the same row of fountains.
By train from Napoli Centrale, then on foot

Trenitalia regional trains to Caserta leave Napoli Centrale dozens of times a day. The journey takes between half an hour and forty minutes, depending on the train and its stops. Buy the regional ticket from the machines at the station or on the Trenitalia app; if it's a paper ticket, remember to validate it.

Caserta station is right opposite the palace. Walk out, cross the avenue and the flowerbeds of Piazza Carlo di Borbone and you're at the main gate: five minutes, no bus, no taxi. It's also why you don't need a car.
Local tip: catch a train that gets in at nine. The palace opens at 8.30am, the coach tours arrive at ten, and the Royal Apartments without the crowds are another thing entirely.
Tickets, opening hours and closed on Tuesdays

The palace is closed on Tuesdays, its weekly day off, and on 25 December. From April to September the Royal Apartments are open 8.30am–7.15pm with last entry at 6.15pm, the park 8.30am–7pm with last entry at 6pm, and the English Garden 8.30am–6pm. From October to March the park closes earlier, with hours that change month by month: the up-to-date table is on the palace's official website. Last entry through the main gate is 6pm regardless.

The full ticket covers the Apartments, the park and the English Garden; there are also palace-only and park-only tickets. Online, the only authorised seller is TicketOne; otherwise buy at the ticket office on the square. You can't leave and come back in on the same ticket, so plan the day in one direction: palace first, then park.

On the first Sunday of every month entry is free, under the Domenica al Museo (Sunday at the Museum) scheme. Two things to know: it's very busy, and that day the English Garden stays closed. If the garden is why you're going, pick another day.
Inside the palace: grand staircase, royal apartments, theatre

Charles of Bourbon commissioned it, laying the first stone in 1752, to have a court that could stand comparison with Versailles, and gave the job to Luigi Vanvitelli. The showstopper is the Scalone d'Onore, the grand staircase: more than a hundred marble steps under a double vault, with lions at the bottom and the octagonal vestibule at the top, where the palace's lines of sight cross. From there you enter the Royal Apartments: the 18th-century rooms with their frescoes, the 19th-century ones redone by the Murats and the Bourbons, the very long throne room, the bedroom of Francis II, and the royal presepe (nativity scene) with hundreds of figures.
