On Saturday and Sunday mornings you can also visit the Teatro di Corte (Court Theatre), thanks to Touring Club volunteers: a small horseshoe theatre with rows of boxes and columns either side of the stage, opened for the carnival of 1769. The Palatine Chapel recalls the chapel at Versailles and holds Mass on Sunday mornings. Allow a couple of hours for the palace.
The park, the waterfall and the English Garden

The park is one long axis of water climbing towards the hill: the Fontana Margherita, then the fountains of the Dolphins, Aeolus, Ceres, and Venus and Adonis, up to the Fountain of Diana and Actaeon at the foot of the Cascata Grande, the great waterfall that drops eighty metres down the rock. From the palace to the waterfall it's about three kilometres on a gentle incline: on foot it takes three quarters of an hour just to get there.

That's why there's an electric shuttle following the waterway, stopping at the fountains of the Dolphins, Aeolus, and Diana and Actaeon: it leaves from the park entrance, runs every day from 9am until the park closes, and a return ticket costs €3. Alternatively, you can hire bikes inside the park, electric ones too, which is the most fun way to do the climb.

Next to the waterfall you enter the English Garden, commissioned by Queen Maria Carolina at the end of the 18th century: rare plants brought from half the world, ponds, fake Roman ruins and the Bath of Venus, with a statue of the goddess rising from the water. It closes before the park, so do it first when you reach the top.

Local tip: go up by shuttle or bike and walk down. On the way down the palace is in front of you the whole time, the row of fountains getting shorter as you go, and the three kilometres pass in about forty minutes.
How to do it with less hassle

Timing first. To do the palace and park properly you need a full day: a couple of hours inside, three or four outside, and lunch in between. If you only have half a day, choose: the Apartments plus a walk to the Fountain of the Dolphins, or the park by bike up to the waterfall. Bring water and a hat, because there's little shade along the central axis and in summer the avenues bake.

If you have time to spare, the palace has two relatives a few kilometres away, which UNESCO included in the same World Heritage Site in 1997. The Belvedere di San Leucio is the silk village founded by Ferdinand IV, with its silk mill and historic looms; the Acquedotto Carolino is Vanvitelli's aqueduct that feeds the waterfall, with the Ponte della Valle and its three tiers of arches. For both you'll need a car or a taxi from the station.

A day at the palace works fine on your own, but if you'd like someone to bring the rooms to life and spare you the queue, there's [the Royal Palace of Caserta in three hours](/esperienze/reggia-di-caserta-in-tre-ore-scalone-appartamenti-e-navetta-al-parco): groups of up to sixteen, the staircase and Apartments with a guide, then the shuttle up to the waterfall and the English Garden.

If palaces and museums are your thing, the rest of Naples' art listings are in the [Art](/categoria/arte) section, and the [map](/mappa) shows where everything is in relation to Napoli Centrale. For other day trips, read our guides to [Pompeii from Naples](/blog/pompei-da-napoli-come-arrivare) and [Capri in a day](/blog/capri-da-napoli-in-giornata).

street-food-napoli-guida-completa.content: Naples is one of the world's capitals of street food. That's not an exaggeration: Neapolitans know it well, and any traveller who wants to understand the real city should try it at least once. Eating standing up in an alley, greaseproof paper in hand, is a ritual with deep roots in Neapolitan culture.
Where to start: the Quartieri Spagnoli

The Quartieri Spagnoli (Spanish Quarter) are the beating heart of Neapolitan street food. The maze of alleys behind Via Toledo is the ideal place to get lost and eat. Here you'll find friggitorie (fry shops) open from dawn, pizza-by-the-slice places baking non-stop and fruit and veg stalls.

items: Cuoppo of mixed fry: fried fish or vegetables in the classic paper cone
Pizza fritta: the fried version of pizza, filled with ricotta and cicoli (pork crackling)
Panzarotti: fried potato croquettes, often with a cheesy centre
Frittatina di pasta: pasta in ragù, shaped into a flat patty and fried
Zeppole salate: soft savoury fritters served hot, straight from the oil
street-food-napoli-guida-completa.content: What to eat in the Quartieri Spagnoli:
Neapolitan breakfast: a ritual worth getting up for

If you think breakfast is a minor meal, Naples will change your mind. The sfogliatella, strictly warm and fresh from the oven, is an almost religious experience. It comes in two versions: riccia (the best known, with crisp, flaky layers) and frolla (softer, made with shortcrust pastry). Both are filled with semolina, ricotta, candied orange and cinnamon.
Get to one of the historic pastry shops in the centre by 8am to find sfogliatelle just out of the oven. After 10am they're not the same.
Porta Nolana market: fish and local flavours

For a proper market experience, Porta Nolana is the place to go. This historic market, one of the oldest in Naples, is famous above all for very fresh fish that comes straight from the fishermen of the bay. There are also stalls of exotic fruit, spices, and Campanian cheeses and cured meats.
In Naples you eat in the street, argue in the street, fall in love in the street. The real city is in the alleys, not in the restaurants.
Pizza: a subject of its own

Talking about Neapolitan street food without talking about pizza would be heresy. The art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo has been on UNESCO's heritage list since 2017, and for good reason: there's nothing like it in the world. The soft dough, the airy cornicione (the puffy crust), buffalo mozzarella from Campania, San Marzano tomatoes. Every element has its own story.

items: Da Michele: the most famous, only margherita and marinara, always a queue
Sorbillo: modern but true to tradition, great for pizza fritta
Starita: in Materdei, one of the best fried pizzas in the city
Di Matteo: in the heart of Spaccanapoli, where Neapolitans eat every day
street-food-napoli-guida-completa.content: The historic pizzerias worth the queue:
When to go and how to get around

Neapolitan street food has no fixed hours, but some times are better than others. Early morning (7–9am) is for sfogliatelle and coffee at the counter. Mid-morning (10am–12pm) the fry shops get going. Lunch (1–3pm) is peak time for pizza by the slice. Evening (6–9pm) is perfect for a cuoppo or a pizza fritta while you stroll.
To find the best places with a local guide, take a look at our street food tour in the Quartieri Spagnoli: 3 hours, tastings included, maximum 12 people per group.

cosa-fare-a-napoli-gratis.content: Free things to do in Naples is a question we get a lot, and the answer is: quite a few. Here are the places you can see without a ticket, grouped by type: old-town streets, viewpoints and steps, the seafront, churches, markets, free events coming up and a few ideas if you're travelling with children. At the end, an honest section on when it's worth handing over €10 or €20.

Free in Naples doesn't mean second best. The finest thing about the city, namely the city itself, has no ticket office: Spaccanapoli, Piazza del Plebiscito, the Galleria Umberto, the view from San Martino, the sea from Castel dell'Ovo to Mergellina. Museums cost money and some are worth it, but a whole day on foot without spending a cent is enough to understand the place.
On foot through the old town

Day one goes like this: start at Piazza del Gesù and walk Spaccanapoli all the way to Forcella. It's the dead-straight street that slices the old town in two, the one that looks like a crack in the city when you see it from the Vomero hill. In one kilometre you cross two thousand years: the Gesù Nuovo, Santa Chiara, San Domenico Maggiore, and the Duomo (the cathedral) a few steps away. You don't need a map. Getting lost in the side alleys is part of the game.

From via San Biagio dei Librai, head up San Gregorio Armeno, the street of nativity-scene makers. You can browse the workshops for free all year round: shepherds, figurines of whoever is in the news, miniature cribs. In December it's heaving; the rest of the year you can walk it comfortably. At the top is via dei Tribunali, the other decumanus, one of the old Greek-Roman main streets.

Two squares deserve a stop. Leafy Piazza Bellini has Greek walls from the 4th century BC out in the open among the café tables: you can see them from the street without ordering anything. From Piazza Dante, walk down to the Plebiscito along via Toledo, pedestrianised and busy at any hour.
From above: viewpoints and steps

Naples is a vertical city, and the best places to grasp that cost nothing. The first is the San Martino viewpoint on the Vomero, the highest point in town: the whole city is laid out in front of you, the old town with the crack of Spaccanapoli, the port, Vesuvius and, on clear days, Capri. The Certosa (the charterhouse) and the castle next door charge admission; the terrace doesn't.

To get up there you can take the funicular from Montesanto, which costs a ticket, or the steps. The Pedamentina di San Martino is 414 steps down from the viewpoint to Corso Vittorio Emanuele, past vegetable plots and glimpses over the rooftops. The Petraio winds down from the Vomero to Chiaia between Art Nouveau villas and gardens you can't see from the road. Then there's the Calata San Francesco and, behind Capodimonte, the Moiariello. They're monuments like any other, just without a ticket office.
Do the steps downhill in the morning, in comfortable shoes: ride the funicular up and walk down. In summer the sun is fierce after 11am and there's little shade.
The sea and the seafront

The Lungomare Caracciolo is pedestrianised from Castel dell'Ovo to Mergellina: flat, wide, with Vesuvius on one side and Posillipo on the other. It's the classic Saturday-afternoon and evening stroll. Start at the Borgo Marinari, the little harbour at the foot of the castle, and walk to Mergellina.

Halfway along is the Villa Comunale, the public garden between the Riviera di Chiaia and the sea: benches, trees, room for children to run. If you want to keep going, carry on towards Posillipo, with views of the bay at every bend. At the far end, at Marechiaro, is Gaiola beach: small, free and with limited numbers, booked online. Just offshore are the islet and the underwater park, with Roman ruins a few metres from the shore.
Squares, arcades and churches open to all

Piazza del Plebiscito is the city's largest square and you can cross it for free at any hour: the colonnade of San Francesco di Paola on one side, the façade of the Palazzo Reale with statues of kings in its niches on the other. The palace charges admission; the square doesn't. A hundred metres away is the Galleria Umberto I, the shopping arcade with its glass-and-iron dome: walk straight in and remember to look up.

The old-town churches are free to visit, apart from their museum sections. The Gesù Nuovo, Santa Chiara, San Domenico Maggiore, the Duomo: in you go, have a look, out you come. The majolica-tiled cloister of Santa Chiara does charge, as do the Cappella Sansevero with the Veiled Christ, the MANN (the archaeological museum), Capodimonte, Napoli Sotterranea and the Galleria Borbonica. If you have a budget, that's where it should go. But the free churches will fill a whole morning.

The Real Bosco di Capodimonte is a case apart: the museum with Caravaggio and the Farnese collection has a ticket, the park around it doesn't. It's 134 hectares of avenues where Neapolitans go running and have picnics.
Markets and neighbourhood streets

The Pignasecca, behind via Toledo, is the city's oldest street market: fish on ice, fruit stalls, fry shops, delis with that day's mozzarella, vendors shouting prices in dialect. Wander it on your own, for free, in the morning. A tarallo (a crunchy ring-shaped biscuit) and a lemonade cost a few coins.

From via Toledo, climb into the Quartieri Spagnoli, the grid of alleys built in the 16th century to house Spanish troops: washing on the lines, scooters, little shops and, on via Emanuele De Deo, the giant Maradona mural, which always has a crowd in front of it. Thirty years ago it was off limits; today you can wander it calmly by day, eyes turned upwards.

items: The Rione Sanità, below the bridge, with its Baroque palazzi and memories of Totò, the great Neapolitan comic actor: for decades locals avoided it, and today it's one of the liveliest parts of the city.
The Borgo Marinari at sunset, sitting on the rocks below Castel dell'Ovo.
cosa-fare-a-napoli-gratis.content: Other streets worth a walk that cost nothing:
Free events coming up

Every week there are neighbourhood festivals, open-air concerts, guided walks and special free openings. The trick is hearing about them in time. In our listings, free events are marked «Free» next to the title, and the listings are updated every morning: the [weekend events](/cosa-fare/weekend) page is the place to plan, and [what to do today](/cosa-fare/oggi) is for last-minute decisions.

A few examples from the time of writing, September 2026. Vespero Napoletano, the city council's slow-tourism festival, brings walks, workshops and concerts to the neighbourhoods every weekend until 24 October, free while places last. Giro Giro Napoli offers free guided tours and children's workshops in museums every Saturday morning until 19 December. On 19 September, the feast of San Gennaro, the Duomo is open to everyone for the miracle of the blood: get there early, it fills up from the morning. The dates change, the method doesn't: check the listings and book where needed.
Free with children

With children, free things often work better than paid ones: no stress about a wasted ticket. The seafront with the Villa Comunale is the easiest: they run, you watch the boats, you turn back when everyone's tired. San Gregorio Armeno with its miniature nativity scenes holds small children's attention for an hour. The Bosco di Capodimonte has big lawns and no cars.

Children like the San Martino viewpoint too, especially if you go up by funicular. And the listings include free Saturday-morning tours designed for families. We've written a separate guide on [things to do in Naples with kids](/blog/cosa-fare-a-napoli-con-i-bambini), covering the paid activities that are really worth it and the ones to skip.
When it's worth paying

Let's be honest: some things in Naples make more sense with €10 or €20 in hand. Not the big museums, which deserve an article of their own, but the small places where a guide changes what you see. Four suggestions, all under €25.

items: The [Veiled Christ with a guide](/esperienze/cristo-velato-e-macchine-anatomiche-con-guida), €15 with ticket and licensed guide, 45 minutes: Sanmartino's statue and the anatomical machines, without the queue that eats an afternoon if you haven't booked.

[The Petraio and the hidden steps](/esperienze/il-petraio-e-le-scale-nascoste-tra-vomero-e-montesanto), €19.50 with funicular and local guide, 2 hours: you can do the steps for free, but with someone from the neighbourhood you take the right ones and see how the city fits together.

[Six stops at the Pignasecca](/esperienze/sei-tappe-nel-mercato-piu-antico-della-citta-caffe-al-limoncello-compres), €25 with six tastings, 2 hours: you can walk the market for free, but with someone who knows the stallholders by name you actually get to taste everything.
cosa-fare-a-napoli-gratis.content: The four spends we recommend after a day of free wandering:
Almost all activities can be cancelled free of charge up to 24 hours before; prices are our partner platforms' current ones.

If you have one day and a small budget, spend the morning on foot in the old town, put the €15 towards the Veiled Christ, and keep the afternoon for San Martino and the evening for the seafront. You don't need anything else.
Where to start

Free Naples is a city you walk: from the old town to the Vomero steps, from the Plebiscito to the sea. What changes every day are the events and special openings, and for those there are the listings. Start from the [things to do in Naples](/cosa-fare) page, where you'll find today's and this weekend's events with «Free» next to the ones that cost nothing, and the [experiences](/esperienze) sorted by price for when you decide to spend.

sagre-ottobre-2026-napoli-dintorni.content: In October, Campania eats out of town. Chestnuts, porcini, black truffles and grapes all arrive at once, and every inland village sets up its stalls in the old centre for a sagra, a local food festival. The big ones can all be done as a day trip from Naples: leave in the afternoon, have dinner in the square, be home by night.

Two things to know before you go. First: without a car it's almost always hard going, because the villages sit on hills or mountains and public transport doesn't reach them in the evening. Second: sagre live on weekends. On weekdays they open in the evening, if at all; on Saturday and Sunday they start at lunchtime and carry on late. Below you'll only find festivals with a 2026 edition confirmed by the town council, the Pro Loco (the local tourist association) or local papers. Where dates aren't out yet, we say so.
Cusano Mutri: the Sagra dei Funghi

This is the longest and best-known festival in the Sannio area. The 46th edition runs from Fri 25 September to Sun 18 October 2026, so it starts today. This year's theme, according to the council, is «Funghi. Un universo in connessione» (Mushrooms: a connected universe): alongside the food there are exhibitions, installations, talks and excursions between the old town and the Matese mountains.

Cusano is a medieval village clinging to the slopes of the Matese, in the province of Benevento: stone houses, steep lanes, cellars and courtyards that turn into taverns during the festival. The star is the porcino from the surrounding woods, in every form: on pasta, fried, in soup, grilled. Alongside it you'll find cured meats and cheeses from the Matese and wine from the Sannio.

The published 2026 opening hours: Monday to Thursday 7pm–midnight, Friday 7pm–1am, Saturday and Sunday 10am–1am. It's about 95km from Naples: allow an hour and a half on the road, more on a Saturday evening.

Local tip: this year the council has introduced a parking booking system, with shuttles into the centre. Book before you set off and, if you can, go on a weekday or for Sunday lunch: on Saturday night the lanes are packed and the queues at the stalls are long. Comfortable shoes, because it's uphill.
Roccamonfina: chestnuts and porcini in a volcano

In the province of Caserta, inside the crater of an extinct volcano, Roccamonfina celebrates its PGI chestnut together with the porcino mushroom. According to the 2026 calendar in the local papers, the festival runs every weekend from 3 October to 1 November, centred on piazza Nicola Amore. The detailed programme isn't out yet: check the Pro Loco's page before you go.

The highlight is the giant pan for caldarroste (roast chestnuts), ten and a half metres across, which made it into the Guinness World Records in 2018. Around it are stalls with chestnuts and porcini, hazelnuts, apples and other produce from the Roccamonfina area. From Naples it's about an hour and ten minutes on the motorway, exit Caianello.
Local tip: go on Saturday afternoon and stay until sunset, when the chestnut roasting starts. Sunday lunchtime is the busiest moment.
Irpinia: Serino, Avella and the Bagnoli truffle
In October, Irpinia (the inland province of Avellino) is chestnut country. Three dates, in calendar order.

Serino, Friday 9, Saturday 10 and Sunday 11 October. This is Irpinia's oldest chestnut festival, now in its 49th edition, run by the Pro Loco in the hamlet of Rivottoli. You eat «vrole», the local roast chestnuts, cooked in the virulera (a big roasting drum) in the square, and dishes made with the PGI Serino chestnut. There's also a small chestnut museum in the old bell tower of Sant'Antonio. It's about an hour from Naples.
Local tip: you can't park in Rivottoli. The Pro Loco runs free shuttles from the PIP area and from the Mercato: leave the car there and ride up with them.

Avella, 16–18 and 23–25 October. The 13th Sagra della Castagna e della Nocciola (chestnut and hazelnut festival) takes over the old town for two weekends, organised by the association I Rami del Melo and the Pro Loco Città di Avella. The hazelnut here gave its name to all the others: avellana, Italian for hazelnut, comes from Avella. It's the closest festival on this list, about 45 minutes from Naples.

Bagnoli Irpino, 23–25 October and 30 October–1 November. «Il Nero di Bagnoli» is the 47th Black Truffle Fair, together with the chestnut festival and produce from the Laceno plateau: mushrooms, cheeses, cured meats, sweets. It's organised by the Pro Loco Bagnoli-Laceno in the old town. It's the furthest of the group from Naples, about an hour and a half.
Local tip: in Bagnoli, buying truffles is part of the trip. Bring cash, because not every stall takes cards, and a cool bag if you want to come home with cheese and salami.
Scala: chestnuts above the Amalfi Coast

Scala is the village above Ravello, and its Festa della Castagna, now in its 49th edition, takes place on Saturday and Sunday 10–11 and 17–18 October. The council was already rallying residents and associations in mid-September. There are roast chestnuts, sweets and chestnut dishes, plus the Palio delle Contrade, a contest between the village's six districts.
From Naples, allow a good hour and a half, between the motorway and the hairpin bends of the Chiunzi pass. It's the right festival if you want to see the Amalfi Coast without the August chaos.
Local tip: parking in Scala is scarce. Arrive before lunch, or leave the car in Ravello and do the last stretch on foot or by bus.
Oliveto Citra: the Festa dell'Uva

For those who prefer wine to chestnuts. In the Sele valley, in the province of Salerno, Oliveto Citra holds its 52nd Festa dell'Uva (grape festival) from Friday 2 to Sunday 4 October. It has run since 1973, and the reason to go is the parade floats, covered in mosaics made of grapes, that process through the village. Around them: stalls, folk groups, music. About an hour and twenty minutes from Naples on the motorway.
Local tip: the float parade draws the whole valley. Set off early to find parking and keep some cash for the stalls.
Montella: one to note, but in November

Montella's Festa della Castagna IGP is the biggest in Irpinia, but it usually falls between late October and the first half of November: in 2025 it ran from 31 October to 2 November and from 7 to 9 November. The 2026 dates haven't been announced yet: check the festival's page before making plans. It's about an hour and twenty minutes from Naples.
The October 2026 food festival calendar

items: 25 September–18 October: Sagra dei Funghi, Cusano Mutri (BN)
2–4 October: Festa dell'Uva, Oliveto Citra (SA)
weekends from 3 October to 1 November: Sagra della Castagna IGP e del Fungo Porcino, Roccamonfina (CE)
9–11 October: Sagra della Castagna di Serino IGP, Rivottoli di Serino (AV)
10–11 and 17–18 October: Festa della Castagna, Scala (SA)
16–18 and 23–25 October: Sagra della Castagna e della Nocciola, Avella (AV)
23–25 October and 30 October–1 November: Il Nero di Bagnoli, Bagnoli Irpino (AV)
dates to be confirmed, usually late October–November: Festa della Castagna IGP, Montella (AV)
