Festivals change their hours at the last minute, especially if it rains: check the Pro Loco's page before getting in the car. If you're staying in the city, the [October events listings](/blog/eventi-napoli-ottobre-2026) cover everything happening in Naples, and [Things to do](/cosa-fare) has the experiences you can book.

And if you fancy wine and countryside before the weekend, the [winery lunch on the slopes of Vesuvius](/esperienze/pranzo-in-cantina-sulle-pendici-del-vesuvio) is right on Naples' doorstep and doesn't need a festival as an excuse. More ideas for eating well are in the [Food section](/categoria/food).

ischia-e-procida-da-napoli.content: Ischia and Procida are two different day trips from Naples, even though they sit on the same route. Procida is small: you can cover it on foot and by bus in half a day and still have time for lunch by the harbour. Ischia is more than four times the size of Capri, with thermal spas, castles and six towns: in a day you'll see one slice of it, and it pays to choose which before you board the hydrofoil. Here's where to leave from, what to see on each island and how to get around once you land.
Hydrofoils and ferries: Beverello, Porta di Massa or Pozzuoli
There are three ports for the two islands, and journey times vary quite a bit.

items: Molo Beverello, opposite the Maschio Angioino castle: hydrofoils and fast boats only, run by SNAV, Alilauro and Caremar. Procida takes about forty minutes; Ischia between fifty minutes and just over an hour, depending on the arrival port and whether it stops at Procida on the way.
Calata Porta di Massa, a little further east: the Caremar and Medmar ferries, the ones that also take cars. About an hour to Procida, a good hour and a half to Ischia.

Pozzuoli, in the Campi Flegrei: the shortest crossing. Around half an hour to Procida and about an hour to Ischia, with Caremar, Medmar and some smaller companies. You get there from Naples on the Cumana (a local train line) or on metro line 2.

ischia-e-procida-da-napoli.content: On Ischia, the hydrofoils don't all dock in the same place: most arrive at Ischia Porto, some at Casamicciola and Forio. Read your ticket carefully, because landing in Forio when you wanted the Aragonese Castle means an hour on the bus. Sailings increase in summer and drop from November: up-to-date timetables are on the companies' websites and the ticket-office boards.

Local tip: if you already know when you're coming back, buy a return with the same company and take a photo of the last sailing time. In rough seas the hydrofoils can stay in port, while the ferries usually still run: in that case you come back by ferry, slower but more reliable.
Procida in a day: Corricella, Terra Murata, Chiaiolella

You land at Marina Grande, also called Sancio Cattolico: pastel houses, bars with tables on the quay, fishermen tending their nets. From here, walk up to Terra Murata, the fortified village at the top of the island. It's a twenty-minute climb between tufa walls and lemon trees, and up there you'll find the abbey of San Michele Arcangelo and Palazzo d'Avalos, which served as a prison for more than a century and can now be visited.

From the Terra Murata viewpoint you look down on the Corricella, the fishing village with houses stacked on top of each other, painted pink, yellow and blue: it's Procida's postcard and also where Massimo Troisi's Il Postino was filmed. Take the little steps down, walk along the tiny harbour and stop to eat there: fish of the day, and Procida lemon in a salad with mint and chilli.

In the afternoon, cross the island to the Chiaiolella on the other side, with its long beach and the bridge to the islet of Vivara, a nature reserve. Get there on the EAV buses: lines L1 and L2 link the port with the Chiaiolella, and the C2 passes Terra Murata and the Corricella. Buy your ticket before boarding, at a tabaccheria (tobacconist) or the kiosks at the port.

Local tip: Procida's streets are narrow, often without pavements, and cars and scooters squeeze through anyway. Wear comfortable shoes and do the climb to Terra Murata in the morning, before the sun hits the walls: the rest of the island is almost all flat.
Ischia in a day: Aragonese Castle, Ischia Ponte, spas and gardens

If it's your first time, get off at Ischia Porto and head to Ischia Ponte: half an hour on foot along the main street, or a few minutes by bus. The Aragonese Castle sits on an islet joined to the mainland by a 15th-century stone bridge. Inside are the roofless cathedral of the Assunta, the convent of the Poor Clares with its cemetery where the nuns were left seated to decompose, and terraces over the sea. A lift cut into the rock takes you to the top. The castle is open every day from morning to sunset, except during maintenance between January and early March: current prices and hours are on the official website.

The second way to spend the day is spas and gardens. The Negombo thermal park, in the bay of San Montano at Lacco Ameno, has hot-water pools set in a botanical garden, plus a beach: it's seasonal, opening in spring and closing in early October, so check the exact closing date before you go. In Forio are the Giardini La Mortella, created by Susana Walton, wife of the composer William Walton: in 2026 they're open from 2 April to 1 November, on Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays and Sundays, 9am–7pm, last entry 6pm.

On the island you get around by EAV bus. The two circular lines, CS and CD, go all the way round Ischia in opposite directions and stop in every town; other lines cover shorter stretches. At summer peak times they're crowded, but they work.

Local tip: if you want the spa and the castle on the same day, take a hydrofoil that arrives at Casamicciola or Forio, spend the morning at Negombo or La Mortella, and leave in the afternoon from Ischia Porto, passing through Ischia Ponte. That way you don't double back.
Is it worth doing both?

Procida and Ischia are fifteen to thirty minutes apart by sea and sailings are frequent, so technically you can. The problem is time on land: if you do Procida in the morning and Ischia in the afternoon, on Ischia you only get a rushed look at the port and the castle. If you have one day, pick one. Procida if you want to walk, take photos and eat well without hurrying; Ischia if you want a hot soak or the castle.

If you do want to see both, the sea is the way to do it. [Ischia and Procida by boat with swims and lunch on board](/esperienze/ischia-e-procida-in-barca-con-bagni-e-pranzo-a-bordo) leaves Beverello by hydrofoil and carries on from Procida by boat with a skipper: the Corricella seen from the water, Ischia's volcanic coastline, swimming stops and lunch on board.
Other islands and day trips from Naples

If your trip has room for another day at sea, read our guide to [Capri from Naples in a day](/blog/capri-da-napoli-in-giornata); if you prefer history, the one for [Pompeii from Naples](/blog/pompei-da-napoli-come-arrivare). All the boat trips and out-of-town excursions are in the [Outdoor](/categoria/outdoor) section, and the [Naples map](/mappa) shows the Molo Beverello and the Calata Porta di Massa in relation to your hotel.

piedigrotta-2026-la-festa-continua-fino-.content: If you were in Mergellina on Tuesday 8 September and heard firecrackers, it wasn't a football match. It was Piedigrotta, the festival Naples has been celebrating since before the word tourism existed. It's documented as far back as the 15th century as the feast of Santa Maria della Grotta, named after the basilica at the mouth of the Crypta Neapolitana, the Roman tunnel that linked the city to Pozzuoli.
This year the programme lasted a whole week, across church, theatre and square. Here's what happened and, above all, what's still on the calendar until 22 September.

The religious heart of it is still the Basilica di Santa Maria di Piedigrotta, at piazza Piedigrotta 24. On 8 September it opened with 9am Mass, the midday supplica (a prayer of petition to the Virgin) and the solemn 7pm Mass, led by the Archbishop of Naples, Cardinal Domenico Battaglia. Free entry, as always. The following Sunday, 13 September, the festival closed in the street with the children's parade in Mergellina at 10.30am and the homage to the Madonna.
Viviani at the Trianon, for a week

At the Teatro Trianon Viviani in piazza Calenda, the 2026–2027 season opened with Raffaele Viviani's "Festa di Piedigrotta", the two-act folk pageant written in 1919. Directed by Nello Mascia, with musical arrangements by Eugenio Bennato. It ran every evening at 9pm from 8 to 12 September, with the final performance on Sunday 13 at 6pm. If you missed it, note the name of the new artistic director, Pierpaolo Sepe: the season he has programmed has only just begun.

On Friday 11 and Saturday 12 September, Piazza Mercato hosted the 24th Notte della Tammorra: two evenings of folk music, tammorre (large frame drums) and dancing, in the square that for centuries was the market and the stage of the lower city. It's the event that reminds everyone each year that the tarantella isn't a postcard, it's something people still play.
What you can still see: Piedigrotta Viva

The most interesting part for anyone arriving now is Piedigrotta Viva, six free evenings of storytelling and song in churches linked to devotion to the Virgin Mary, organised by the Campania Region with Scabec. The first was on 11 September in Marano. These remain:

items: Tuesday 15 September, 7.30pm, Basilica di Santa Lucia a Mare, Naples
Wednesday 16 September, 7.15pm, Chiesa di Sant'Anna di Palazzo, Naples
Friday 18 September, 7pm, Chiesa di San Pasquale a Chiaia, Naples
Sunday 20 September, 7pm, Chiesa della SS. Annunziata, Torre del Greco
Tuesday 22 September, 8pm, Chiesa di Santo Strato, Posillipo

piedigrotta-2026-la-festa-continua-fino-.content: On stage, stories from Casillo, Morrone and Enza Barra alternate with the voices of Maglione, Rondi, Malapena, Carfora and Marini. Arrive a quarter of an hour early: these are churches, and seats run out.

Before or after the basilica, pop into the Parco Vergiliano a Piedigrotta, a short walk from Mergellina station. Inside are Leopardi's tomb, the monument that tradition calls Virgil's tomb, and the entrance to the Crypta Neapolitana. Free, and almost always empty.
If after all this you still want live Neapolitan song, the Shows section has the one-hour concert at the Galleria Principe di Napoli: voice and instruments without microphones, every evening.

aperitivo-napoli-dove-andare.content: In Naples, aperitivo (the pre-dinner drink) is an institution, but it works differently from northern Italy. There's no Milan-style buffet culture. You order a drink, something to nibble arrives, you stand outside on the pavement or in a little square, and you talk. A lot. For hours.

items: Campari Spritz: more bitter than the Aperol version, and more Neapolitan
Limoncello spritz: made with craft limoncello from the Amalfi Coast, very refreshing
Falanghina dei Campi Flegrei: a local white wine, little known but excellent
Gin and tonic with Vesuvius herbs: the local take on the classic
Americano: vermouth and Campari, the timeless classic

aperitivo-napoli-dove-andare.content: Every neighbourhood has its own scene. Chiaia is smarter and more polished. The Quartieri Spagnoli are more down-to-earth and less touristy. The Vomero is where young Neapolitans go. The Riviera di Chiaia, with bars looking out to sea, is perfect for sunset.
The right time is between 6.30pm and 8.30pm. Earlier is too early; later, Neapolitans are already at dinner. The magic happens in that window.

A Neapolitan aperitivo often comes with small snacks included in the price of the drink: taralli 'nzogna e pepe (crunchy rings made with lard and pepper), peanuts, Gaeta olives, slices of provolone del Monaco cheese. In some old-town bars you'll also get crostini with stracciatella or pistachio pesto.
A Neapolitan aperitivo isn't a meal. It's a philosophy. It's the moment the city slows down, looks around and remembers it's alive.

cosa-fare-a-napoli-la-sera.content: Evenings in Naples start late. At 8pm the restaurants are half empty, by 9.30pm there’s a queue outside, and people head out just when everyone elsewhere is heading home. Before dinner there’s aperitivo, after dinner the passeggiata, the evening stroll that is the city’s real night-time activity. If you usually eat at seven, shift everything by two hours.

The second thing to know is that a Neapolitan evening happens in the street. You don’t need a bar: a square, a low wall by the sea or an alley with tables outside will do. This guide goes area by area, because each one has its own kind of evening, and finishes with what you can book: a street food walk after sunset, a concert of Neapolitan song with no microphones, three hours on a boat while the sun drops behind Posillipo.
The seafront and Castel dell’Ovo

The simplest and most Neapolitan evening: via Caracciolo has been pedestrianised for years, it’s flat, with the sea on one side and the Villa Comunale park on the other. You walk from Piazza Vittoria to Mergellina, and halfway along is the Borgo Marinari, the little harbour at the foot of Castel dell’Ovo, where people sit on the jetty with their feet towards the water and the floodlit castle overhead. Behind you, Vesuvius, with the lights of the towns on its slopes.

The right time is sunset onwards: families with pushchairs, teenagers with beers, runners, people taking photos with the castle behind them. It’s free, and it goes well with a late dinner in the lanes of Santa Lucia or an ice cream eaten on the move.
Piazza Bellini and the old town

A tree-lined square two minutes from via Tribunali, with Greek walls from the 4th century BC exposed in the open between the café tables. From 7pm it fills with students, people coming out of the bookshops and live music drifting from the bars around it. It’s where Neapolitans go for a drink before dinner, and they often stay until well after.

From there you can walk the whole old town. At night via Tribunali and Spaccanapoli are a different city from the daytime one: the nativity-scene shops of San Gregorio Armeno close, and what’s left are the fry shops, pizzerias with people waiting outside and the open doorways of old palazzi. Piazza San Domenico Maggiore and Piazza del Gesù are the two natural stops. If you’d rather someone showed you round, there’s the [tasting walk that starts from Piazza Bellini](/esperienze/polpette-spritz-e-mura-greche-giro-di-assaggi-da-piazza-bellini): meatballs, spritz and the Greek walls, two and a half hours for €39.
Chiaia and the baretti

Chiaia is the smart neighbourhood between via dei Mille and the sea, and at night the action is packed into a few lanes behind Piazza dei Martiri: vico Belledonne, via Bisignano, via Ferrigni. Locals call them the baretti, the little bars, and the name says it all: tiny places, people standing outside glass in hand, the whole lane turning into one bar. You go after dinner, between 11pm and 1am, and drift from one lane to the next with no plan.

It’s the best-dressed part of town, but nobody will look twice at your trainers. From the seafront it’s five minutes uphill from Piazza Vittoria; from Vomero, take the funicular. If you want something cheaper and more down to earth, the [old town pub crawl with street music](/esperienze/giro-dei-pub-del-centro-storico-con-la-musica-di-strada) is on the other side of the city: two and a half hours for €18, walking the alleys with a group and ending up wherever the band is playing.
Vomero and the viewpoints at night

Vomero is the hill above Chiaia, and in the evening people go up for one reason: to look down on Naples. The viewpoint in front of the Certosa di San Martino is an open public terrace that takes in the whole lower city, the old town with the long cut of Spaccanapoli, the port and Vesuvius. At night the lights trace the shape of the bay better than any map. Next door is Castel Sant’Elmo, the six-pointed star of volcanic tuff stone whose terrace is open during the day.

You go up by funicular (a cable railway up the hillside) from Montesanto, Chiaia or via Toledo, or on foot via the Pedamentina, 414 steps that lead from the centre straight to the Certosa. If your legs are up to it, come down the Petraio, the stairway from Vomero to Chiaia past villas and glimpses of the sea: it’s poorly lit at night, so do it at sunset and reach the bottom in time for dinner. Via Scarlatti and the streets around it have a neighbourhood kind of evening, quieter than the centre.
Eating late: street food and pizzerias

In Naples dinner starts after 9pm, which makes life easy if you’re running late. Pizza is the evening meal par excellence: you take a number, wait outside with everyone else, and the pizza comes out of the oven in a few minutes. The wait is part of the ritual.

The alternative is eating as you walk. Pizza a portafoglio (a small pizza folded in four), frittatina di pasta (a deep-fried pasta patty), a cuoppo (a paper cone of fried bits), pizza fritta: Neapolitan street food costs a few euros a stop and you’ll find it along via Tribunali, in the Pignasecca market and the Quartieri Spagnoli. The hard part is knowing where to go in. The [old town street food tour with a local guide](/esperienze/street-food-nel-centro-storico-con-una-guida-del-posto) sorts that out in two and a half hours: six or seven tastings in the right shops, spritz and limoncello included, €42. Go on an empty stomach and don’t book dinner afterwards.

Sfogliatella, the ridged, shell-shaped pastry filled with ricotta, is best eaten warm and knows no hours: some bakeries keep baking them late into the night, from the station to Mergellina. If you pass one with a queue after midnight, join it.
Live music and shows

Neapolitan song was born for bare voices and mandolins, and concerts like that still happen: fifty-seat rooms in the centre, singers a metre away, no amplification, and the story behind each piece told between songs. [An hour of Neapolitan song without microphones](/esperienze/unora-di-canzone-napoletana-senza-microfoni) takes place in the Galleria Principe di Napoli, lasts an hour, costs €20 with a drink included and needs booking in advance. The same room also hosts [Napulitanata, tarantella and classics sung unamplified](/esperienze/napulitanata-tarantella-e-classici-a-voce-nuda), same price, for those who want the more upbeat version.

Then there’s everything that changes week to week: open-air concerts in summer, late museum openings in autumn, opera in courtyards, theatre. As we write, for example, the Archaeological Museum opens in the evening on Thursdays in October with live music among the statues, for €10, and the ruins of Pompeii open at night on Fridays and Saturdays for €7. The shows we follow, with date, time and price checked at the source, are in the [shows section of the programme](/categoria/spettacoli).
Sunset from the sea

You should see Naples from the water at least once, and evening is the best time. The small nine-seat boats leave from the jetty on via Caracciolo and follow the Posillipo coast: villas on the sea, Palazzo Donn’Anna with its foundations in the water, the caves, the Gaiola. Behind you, Vesuvius and the whole city lighting up. You come back in the dark with the seafront lights ahead.

There are two options. [Three hours on a boat at sunset, with spritz and bruschetta](/esperienze/tre-ore-in-barca-al-tramonto-con-spritz-e-bruschette) is the most popular: €80, leaving in the late afternoon and staying out until after sunset. If you prefer sailing, there’s the [sunset sail with aperitivo on board](/esperienze/a-vela-verso-il-tramonto-con-aperitivo-a-bordo), two and a half hours from Molo Marinelli at the same price. May to October, sea permitting.
Evenings with children

Naples in the evening works better with children than you might think, because life happens outdoors and everyone eats late anyway. The seafront is the place: pedestrianised, flat, with the Villa Comunale next to it and ice cream along the way. The Borgo Marinari, with its boats and castle, keeps little ones busy for a good hour.

The sunset boat works for them too, if the sea is calm: an hour and a half is about right, three hours is a lot. A pizza-making class in the late afternoon, where you knead the dough and then eat what you made, rounds off the day without having to find a restaurant. More ideas, with ages and durations, are in the [guide to things to do in Naples with kids](/blog/cosa-fare-a-napoli-con-i-bambini).
What to book for the evening

items: Old town street food with a local guide: two and a half hours, six or seven tastings, €42. Instead of dinner.
An hour of Neapolitan song without microphones: a fifty-seat room in the Galleria Principe di Napoli, one hour after dinner, €20 with a drink.
Three hours on a boat at sunset with spritz and bruschetta: from the via Caracciolo jetty along Posillipo, €80, May to October.
Old town pub crawl with street music: two and a half hours in the alleys, €18, if you want to meet people.
Meatballs, spritz and Greek walls from Piazza Bellini: the long aperitivo, two and a half hours, €39.
cosa-fare-a-napoli-la-sera.content: Our pick of evening experiences, with price and duration. You book online and nearly all can be cancelled free up to 24 hours before.
What about tonight?

Whatever changes daily, concerts, late openings, neighbourhood festivals, is in the programme, updated every morning with time, place and price checked at the source. If you’re in Naples now and want to know what’s on in a few hours, open [things to do in Naples today](/cosa-fare/oggi) and take your pick.

One last tip: public transport thins out in the evening and the funiculars run reduced hours. If you go up to Vomero after dinner, check how you’ll get down first, or be ready for the Pedamentina steps on foot.

cosa-fare-a-napoli-con-i-bambini.content: Naples works better with children than you might think, on one condition: give them things to do, not things to look at. Baroque churches and paintings hold them for twenty minutes; kneading pizza dough, a boat bouncing on the waves, a tunnel underground or a fish staring back through the glass hold them for hours. This guide is built that way: first things to do, then things to see, and at the end the practical stuff, which matters more in Naples than elsewhere.
We’ve put together fifteen ideas we’ve tried, grouped by type. Where there’s a bookable experience we say so, with the booking platform’s price; the rest you can do on your own, often for free.
Doing, not looking: pizza-making classes

The thing that always works, at any age, is a pizza class. Flour, water, yeast, dough stretched by hand (no rolling pin, as Neapolitan rules demand), the oven, and an hour later you eat what you made. Children come out with floury faces and a new skill; parents with a technique to try at home. Almost all the classes in the centre also make tiramisù while the dough rises, and the «pizza and gelato in two hours» format is designed for families with small children and not much patience.
A tip: book the midday slot. You arrive hungry, eat your own pizza for lunch and keep the afternoon free for the sea or a walk.
The sea, which in Naples is right in town

From Castel dell’Ovo to Mergellina the seafront is pedestrianised, flat and two kilometres long: bring the pushchair, the scooter or a bike, with the obligatory stop at the Borgo Marinari, the little harbour at the foot of the castle, where children watch the boats and the cats. The castle, when it’s open, is free to visit, and from its terraces you can see the whole bay.

To actually get out on the water there are boats: the tour of the bay in an hour and a quarter, taking in Vesuvius, Posillipo and Nisida from offshore, is the short version; trips of two or three hours with a swim stop in the coves of Posillipo and at the Gaiola are the long one, May to October. Children who have never seen Naples from the sea suddenly understand why the city is built in staircases.
Underground

Naples has a second city beneath the first, and children like it more than the one on top. The Galleria Borbonica, under Chiaia, has wartime air-raid shelters and vintage cars abandoned in the tunnels: an hour-long guided tour that feels like an adventure. Napoli Sotterranea, from the old town, goes forty metres down into Greek and Roman cisterns, with a few narrow candlelit passages that children remember for years. The catacombs in the Sanità district are fine from about six or seven upwards; the Cimitero delle Fontanelle, with its skulls, is best saved for when they’re older.
Underground it’s cool even in August and it never rains: the perfect fallback for bad days.
Museums that aren’t boring

In Bagnoli there’s Città della Scienza, the science museum with a planetarium and interactive rooms where you can touch everything: a full half day, with space to run around outside. In the Villa Comunale on the seafront, the Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn houses Europe’s oldest aquarium, founded in 1874: period tanks, fish from the bay, octopus and moray eels a few centimetres from the glass. It’s small, so just right for a child’s attention span.

The National Archaeological Museum is huge, but with a strategy it’s manageable: straight to the Egyptian section with the mummies, then the Pompeii mosaics with the «cave canem» dog, then out. With a guide who knows how to talk to children, two hours fly by; on your own, stop at one.
Up high: the funicular and the star-shaped castle

The Montesanto funicular, a cable railway through the hill, is a game in itself: seven minutes climbing inside the hillside and you pop out in Vomero. From there it’s a ten-minute walk to Castel Sant’Elmo, the castle shaped like a six-pointed star with the highest terrace in the city. You can see Vesuvius, the port and Capri, and the rest of Naples suddenly makes sense. Next door, the Certosa di San Martino has a collection of nativity scenes including the Cuciniello, hundreds of figures that children pore over like a comic.
To come down, if legs allow, there’s the Pedamentina: 414 steps past vegetable gardens down to the Quartieri Spagnoli. With the smallest ones, take the funicular again.
Rides, parks and woods

Edenlandia, in Fuorigrotta, is the city’s historic amusement park, opened in the 1960s and brought back to life: old-fashioned rides, the right size for children up to ten, and Neapolitan parents bringing their kids where they used to go themselves. The Villa Comunale has a playground and flowerbeds to run around between visits to the aquarium. The Real Bosco di Capodimonte, at the top of the hill, is a 134-hectare park with lawns, avenues and a museum that won’t take offence if you skip it.
Free on Saturdays: Giro Giro Napoli

Every Saturday morning until December, the city’s museums and cultural sites open to children with free guided visits designed for them: it’s called Giro Giro Napoli and it’s run by the city council. The programme changes every week and must be booked; we list it on the Cosa fare page among the current events, with the link to sign up.
If it rains

items: A pizza or fresh pasta class, indoors and with lunch included
The Galleria Borbonica or Napoli Sotterranea, where nobody cares about the weather outside
The Stazione Zoologica aquarium, small and under cover
The metro’s art stations: Toledo, with its blue mosaic that descends below sea level, is an outing in itself and costs one ticket
The Galleria Umberto I, where you stay dry under a glass-and-iron dome and have a sfogliatella, the shell-shaped ricotta pastry
cosa-fare-a-napoli-con-i-bambini.content: Naples in the rain has a short but good list:
Food, beyond pizza

Children eat everywhere in Naples: pasta al ragù (slow-cooked meat sauce) on Sundays, frittatina di pasta (a deep-fried pasta patty) as a snack, pizza a portafoglio (folded in four) to eat on the go, warm sfogliatella for breakfast, gelato at any hour. Street food tours in the old town are designed for adults but families often join: two and a half hours, six or seven tastings, and nobody complaining they’re hungry.
The practical stuff

items: A pushchair in the old town is hard work: basalt paving stones, steps, crowded alleys. Up to about three, a baby carrier or backpack is better; the pushchair comes into its own on the seafront and in Vomero
Lunch is late and dinner is late: pizzerias open around 7.30pm and fill up by 9pm. If your children flag early, go in as they open
Metro Line 1 and the funiculars cover almost everything in this guide; taxis are the answer with suitcases, buses are not

Bookable experiences list maximum group size, language and duration on their page: with children what counts is the length (over three hours is a gamble) and free cancellation up to 24 hours before, in case someone falls ill
In summer, the proper sea is at Posillipo and the Campi Flegrei; in the city you swim from a boat, not from the beach
cosa-fare-a-napoli-con-i-bambini.content: What matters more in Naples than elsewhere:

A model day with children aged five to ten: pizza class at midday in the centre, funicular up to Vomero in the afternoon for the terrace of Castel Sant’Elmo, down to Chiaia and sunset on the seafront with an ice cream. No museums, no queues, everyone happy.

To find out what’s on while you’re in town, festivals included, see the things to do in Naples page: pick your dates and you’ll find the events and bookable experiences for those days. Classes are in the Workshops category, boats in Outdoor.

cosa-fare-a-napoli-weekend-2-4-ottobre-2.content: The first weekend of October in Naples has three things that happen once a year. Open House throws open more than 150 free visits to palazzi, building sites and private homes that are usually closed. Spinacorona brings Beethoven to ten churches in the old town, free and with no booking. And Sunday 4 is the first Sunday of the month, so state museums are free: MANN, Capodimonte, Palazzo Reale, San Martino. Add the last weekend of the Pessoa Luna Park at Castel Sant’Elmo and Antonacci’s last three nights at Pompeii, and the calendar is full. Below you’ll find it all day by day. The page updated every morning is [this weekend](/cosa-fare/weekend).

From Friday 2 to Sunday 4 October, the eighth Open House Napoli lets anyone into places you normally can’t get into: historic palazzi, building sites, private homes, urban walks. There are around 160 visits, some seventy of them opening for the first time, with 603 volunteers acting as guides. New this year are the ancient theatre of Neapolis at the Anticaglia, San Giovanni a Carbonara with its cloisters, and the Museo Filangieri. On Friday 2 the new Sconfinamenti section adds about twenty visits in the Campi Flegrei. For children there’s OHN Kids at the Santissima, with clay, photography and printing workshops.
It’s all free. Many sites do need booking, though, which opens today, Fri 25 September, at 6pm on openhousenapoli.org. Other sites are walk-in, while space lasts.

Local tip: the most popular Open House visits go within hours. Register on the site before 6pm on Friday, so when booking opens all you have to do is choose. Keep two or three backups: the walk-in sites are plan B.
Friday 2: Beethoven, Timi and Pompeii by night

Spinacorona, the festival run by pianist Michele Campanella, turns ten and devotes the whole edition to Beethoven. On Friday at 6pm Campanella plays at the Biblioteca Universitaria, a concert with commentary. At 9pm the Trio «L’Arciduca» plays in the Basilica della Santissima Annunziata Maggiore. Entry is free with no booking, until seats run out. Doors open half an hour before.

At the Teatro Bellini, Filippo Timi brings his [Amleto²](/eventi/amleto-2-filippo-timi-bellini-2026), a bored Hamlet who turns the tragedy into a circus. It runs 85 minutes. Friday at 8.45pm, Saturday at 7pm, Sunday at 6pm. If you’re heading out of town, there are two evenings at Pompeii. On Fridays and Saturdays the ruins [stay open at night](/eventi/serate-nella-grande-pompei-2026), 7.30pm–11.30pm, €7 per site. At the Teatro Grande, meanwhile, Biagio Antonacci closes his [Unplugged](/eventi/biagio-antonacci-teatro-grande-pompei-2026) tour with three nights in a row, 2–4 October at 9pm.
Saturday 3: Vomero, Capodimonte and four concerts

At 10am the last leg of the [Tour del Giallo](/eventi/tour-del-giallo-vomero-2026) begins, a walk around Vomero through the settings of Maurizio de Giovanni’s crime novels. It’s free, booked by email to redazione@gialli.it, and repeats on Sunday at the same time. Saturday morning also has Giro Giro Napoli’s free visits for children. At 4pm in the Real Bosco di Capodimonte, Bosco in Rosa sets off: a 4km walk at your own pace in aid of the Santobono children’s hospital. You sign up online and pushchairs are welcome.

Spinacorona puts on four concerts in one day. At 12pm, Lieder at Santa Maria di Costantinopoli; at 5pm, the Serenade Op. 8 at San Giovanni a Carbonara. At 7pm Monica Leone plays the piano variations at Sant’Eligio Maggiore, and at 9pm it’s the cello and piano sonatas at Santi Apostoli. In the evening there are also two paid shows. At the Augusteo there’s [Mavi](/eventi/mavi-teatro-augusteo-2026) at 9pm, tickets €26–34.50. At the Palapartenope it’s Maradona, the show: the story of Diego in Naples, a stone’s throw from the stadium that bears his name.
Sunday 4: free museums and Beethoven into the evening

It’s the first Sunday of the month, so state museums and archaeological parks are free. The MANN (National Archaeological Museum) is open 9am–7.30pm, Capodimonte and its park 8.30am–7.30pm, Palazzo Reale 9am–8pm. The Certosa di San Martino opens 8.30am–6.30pm, last entry 5.30pm. Castel Sant’Elmo with the Museo del Novecento and the Floridiana are free too. Outside the city, Pompeii, Herculaneum, Oplontis, Boscoreale, the Flavian Amphitheatre in Pozzuoli, Baia and the Royal Palace of Caserta all take part. Temporary exhibitions are still paid. For MANN and Capodimonte booking isn’t compulsory, but it’s a good idea.

Local tip: on free Sunday at 11am the MANN is as packed as the metro. Go in at opening time or after 4pm. Or head up to Vomero: do San Martino in the morning, have lunch, and in the afternoon walk a few metres over to the Pessoa Luna Park, which opens at 5.30pm. Castel Sant’Elmo and the Certosa sit side by side.

Sunday afternoon belongs to Spinacorona. At 12pm Filippo Gamba plays at San Giovanni a Mare, at 5pm there are violin and piano sonatas at San Pietro a Majella. At 7pm Andrea Padova plays the Diabelli Variations at the Trinità dei Pellegrini. At 9pm the closing concert, with Kyoko Yonemoto and Campanella, returns to the Annunziata. If you’d rather be in the countryside, there’s [Vendemmiamo la Catalanesca](/eventi/vendemmiamo-la-catalanesca-2026) on the slopes of Vesuvius, 9.30am–5pm: grape picking in the morning, then a tasting and lunch among the vines.
Last days and things still running

items: [Pessoa Luna Park](/eventi/pessoa-luna-park-castel-sant-elmo-2026) in the moat of Castel Sant’Elmo: last weekend, Thursday to Sunday 5.30pm–12.30am, €2.50, free for under-18s and over-65s
Maria Lai, «Essere è tessere» at the Madre museum: until 12 October, €8
Serate nella Grande Pompei (Pompeii by night): Fridays and Saturdays until 10 October
Philip Colbert at Pompeii, included in the ruins ticket, until 30 November
Vespero Napoletano: free walks and workshops run by the city council at weekends until 24 October
cosa-fare-a-napoli-weekend-2-4-ottobre-2.content: What closes on Sunday, and what stays on:

With so many places spread across the centre, Vomero and Capodimonte, the [map of Naples](/mappa) helps you line up your stops without crossing the city three times. The rest of October is in [Naples events in October 2026](/blog/eventi-napoli-ottobre-2026). For any other day, [Things to do in Naples](/cosa-fare) shows the events and bookable experiences on the dates you choose.

napoli-sotterranea-tunnel-greci.content: When you walk along Spaccanapoli or through piazza San Gaetano, you’re on streets built over thousands of years of history. Forty metres down there is quite literally another city: tunnels dug by the Greeks in the 4th century BC, enlarged by the Romans, used as aqueducts in the Middle Ages, turned into storage in the 1800s and finally used as air-raid shelters in the Second World War.
Greek origins: Neapolis and the tunnels

Naples began as a Greek colony, Neapolis, the new city, around 470 BC. The Greeks needed stone to build walls and roads. They started quarrying Neapolitan yellow tuff, a light but strong volcanic stone, creating underground galleries that over time became the backbone of the city’s water supply.

items: Tuff quarry galleries from the 4th–3rd century BC
Roman cisterns from the 1st–2nd century AD
Medieval passages of the Graeco-Roman aqueduct
Graffiti and writing left by people sheltering during the 1943 bombings
A theatre room carved into the tuff, used by the shelterers for performances
napoli-sotterranea-tunnel-greci.content: What you’ll find in the tunnels:

The Romans turned the Greek tunnels into a sophisticated water system serving the whole city. The Augustan aqueduct, built in the 1st century BC, carried water from the Serino springs to the underground cisterns of Naples. The system stayed in use until 1885, when a cholera epidemic pushed the authorities to build a new, modern aqueduct.
Naples is a city in layers. You can’t understand the present unless you know everything underneath it, literally.
The Second World War: air-raid shelters

Between 1940 and 1944 Naples was one of the most heavily bombed cities in Italy. The galleries became a refuge for civilians during air raids, with thousands of people at a time sheltering in the tuff cavities. They lived there for weeks: sleeping on wooden bunks, cooking on makeshift stoves, setting up small theatres and chapels.

The shelters have survived almost intact: you’ll still see graffiti on the walls, children’s scribbles and the traces of everyday life underground. Some original objects have been left where they were.

items: Entrance: piazza San Gaetano 68, in the heart of Spaccanapoli
Guided tour length: about 80 minutes
Temperature in the tunnels: a constant 15°C (bring a jumper)
Some passages are narrow: if you’re claustrophobic you can skip them
Recommended minimum age: 6

napoli-sotterranea-tunnel-greci.content: Visiting Napoli Sotterranea is more than a tourist tour: it’s a way to understand what makes this city what it is. The resilience, the knack for adapting, the layers of culture. It all makes more sense when you walk where the Greeks walked 2,500 years ago.

workshop-ceramica-napoli.content: Campania has a ceramics tradition going back thousands of years. The majolica (tin-glazed pottery) of Vietri sul Mare, the porcelain of Capodimonte, the terracotta of the coast: each area has its own style, techniques and motifs. In Naples this tradition lives on in a network of artisan workshops scattered between the old town and the outskirts.

The Real Fabbrica di Capodimonte, the royal porcelain factory, was founded in 1743 by Charles of Bourbon, who wanted to rival Meissen porcelain. The hallmarks of Capodimonte porcelain, its whiteness, floral reliefs and mythological figures, are recognised worldwide. Some masters still hand down these techniques today in workshops open to the public.

items: Throwing on an electric wheel
Hand-building (pinch pots, coils, slabs)
Decorating with oxides and glazes
The basics of firing in gas and wood kilns
The history of Campanian ceramics
workshop-ceramica-napoli.content: What you learn in a ceramics workshop:

In the old town, around via San Gregorio Armeno, the famous street of nativity-scene makers, several workshops open their doors for courses and classes. Some focus on the presepe (nativity scene) tradition, others teach majolica work with the typical coloured glazes.
Ceramics workshops are fine even if you’ve never touched clay. No experience needed: the masters guide you step by step. Wear clothes you don’t mind getting dirty.

The best part of a workshop is that at the end you take home the piece you made, once it’s been fired. There’s something deeply satisfying about getting home knowing there’s a mug, a plate or a vase on your shelf that you made with your own hands in a Neapolitan workshop.
Clay doesn’t lie. If you’re distracted, the pot collapses. If you’re present, something beautiful emerges. It’s the most honest lesson I’ve ever had.
Have a look at our ceramics and mosaic workshops in the old town: 2–3 hours with a master craftsman, materials included, and a piece to take home.

pompei-da-napoli-come-arrivare.content: Pompeii is half an hour from Naples by train and makes an easy day trip, no coach or tour needed, as long as you know three things: which station to leave from, which ticket to buy and which gate to go in by. Below you'll find the journey, the tickets, a four-to-five-hour route through the ruins and how to pair it with Herculaneum or Vesuvius.
How to get to Pompeii from Naples

The easiest way is the Circumvesuviana, the local commuter railway run by EAV, on its Naples–Sorrento line. It leaves from Porta Nolana, stops at Garibaldi (underneath Napoli Centrale, the main station) and in just over half an hour drops you at Pompei Scavi-Villa dei Misteri. The Porta Marina entrance is a stone's throw from the platform: step out, cross over and you're in the queue. Buy your ticket at the station or on the EAV app, or tap a contactless card at the gates that take Tap&Go. Remember to tap out too, or the fare won't be calculated properly.

Watch out for the wrong line. Trains to Poggiomarino also go through Pompeii, but they stop at Pompei Santuario, near the Piazza Anfiteatro entrance on the other side of the site. That works too, as long as you know. You'll spot the Sorrento trains on the departures board.

The alternative is Trenitalia, the national railway: regional trains on the Naples–Salerno line stop at Pompei station, in the modern town, and from there the Pompei Link service takes you to the ruins. On Sundays, in the periods when it runs, there's also a Rome–Pompeii Frecciarossa (high-speed train) that stops at Napoli Centrale at 10.13am and reaches Pompeii at 10.40am, returning from Pompeii at 6.40pm. Handy if you're coming from Rome for the day; before you count on it, check on the Trenitalia website that it's running that Sunday.

Local tip: the Circumvesuviana is a commuter train, not a tourist one. Skip the 8am trains, take one between 8.30 and 9am and you'll arrive at opening time once the commuters have thinned out. Same on the way back: after 5pm the carriages fill up.
Tickets, opening hours and rules: what to know first
The site opens every day at 9am. Until 14 October it closes at 7pm, last entry 5.30pm; from 15 October to 15 March it closes at 5pm, last entry 3.30pm. It's only closed on 25 December and 1 January.
These are the tickets in force since 12 January 2026, according to the official website, pompeiisites.org:

items: €20: the ancient city only, without the suburban villas.
€25: the ancient city plus the Villa dei Misteri and Villa di Diomede, Villa Regina at Boscoreale with its Antiquarium, and the shuttle bus.
€30: all of the above plus Oplontis, the Stabiae villas and the Stabiae museum, valid for three days.
Reduced to €2 for EU citizens aged 18 to 25.

pompei-da-napoli-come-arrivare.content: The detail that catches lots of people out: the Villa dei Misteri (Villa of the Mysteries) isn't included in the €20 ticket. If you want to see the red frescoes of the Dionysian rite, get the €25 one. Tickets are in your name, you'll be asked for ID at the entrance and they're valid for one entry only, so no popping out for lunch and coming back. There's a cap of 20,000 visitors a day: buy online on Vivaticket, the channel the Park recommends, especially at weekends. Rucksacks and bags can be no bigger than 30x30x15cm; anything larger goes in the left-luggage.

Entry is free on the first Sunday of the month, and the next one is 4 October. Free also means crowds: if you only have one day and can choose, a Tuesday or Wednesday with a ticket is better. The Park publishes how free Sundays work on its Orari e tariffe (hours and prices) page: check it a few days before.
Round the ruins: four or five hours without doubling back

Pompeii is a real city, not a museum: it's a couple of kilometres of Roman paving stones from one end to the other, and which houses are open changes through the year. Pick up the map at the entrance or download it from the website, because it shows what you can visit that day. This is a route that works, from Porta Marina to the Amphitheatre.
The Forum and the Basilica

You enter at Porta Marina, walk uphill and five minutes later you're in the Forum, the long square with Vesuvius in the background. Around it are the Temple of Jupiter, the Basilica where justice was administered and the granaries holding the plaster casts of the victims. Allow half an hour.
Casa del Fauno and Villa dei Misteri

From the Forum head north to the Casa del Fauno (House of the Faun), the largest house in the city, with the bronze statuette of the dancing faun in the impluvium, the rainwater basin in the atrium. The Alexander mosaic that covered the floor is now at MANN, the archaeological museum in Naples, but the house makes perfect sense without it. Then leave through Porta Ercolano and walk along Via dei Sepolcri, the street of tombs, to the Villa dei Misteri, outside the walls: ten minutes on foot, and the room with the red-background frieze is worth the €25 ticket on its own.
The Stabian Baths and the two theatres

Head back towards the centre and take Via dell'Abbondanza, the main street. The Terme Stabiane (Stabian Baths) are the oldest in the city: changing rooms, hot and cold rooms, stucco ceilings. A little further down are the Teatro Grande, which held a few thousand people, and the Odeion, the small covered theatre for music. Five minutes sitting on the steps is the best way to rest your legs.
Via dell'Abbondanza to the Amphitheatre

From here walk east along Via dell'Abbondanza, past shops, thermopolia (Roman takeaway counters with jars sunk into the bar) and election slogans painted on the walls. At the end you'll find the Palestra Grande (Great Gymnasium) and the Amphitheatre, the oldest Roman stone amphitheatre still standing. Leave by Piazza Anfiteatro and you're close to Pompei Santuario station, with no need to cross the whole city again.

Local tip: the sun is the real enemy. There's little shade in Pompeii and the stones give off the heat even at the end of September. Closed shoes with thick soles, no sandals, a hat and a water bottle: there are drinking fountains inside the site and the water is good. Bring a sandwich by all means, but you can only eat in the designated areas.
Pompeii with Herculaneum or Vesuvius

If you've energy to spare, the trip can stretch in two directions. The first is Herculaneum (Ercolano), on the same Circumvesuviana line at the Ercolano Scavi stop, halfway between Naples and Pompeii. It's smaller and takes two hours, but it's better preserved: the volcanic mud sealed in wood, upper floors and colours. Pompeii in the morning and Herculaneum in the afternoon is doable, but at a brisk pace and without the Villa dei Misteri. If you want to see both with someone explaining what you're looking at, there's [Herculaneum with an archaeologist, ticket included](/esperienze/ercolano-con-un-archeologo-biglietto-incluso), two hours in a small group.

The second is Vesuvius, the volcano behind all of this. Climbing to the crater and then going down to Pompeii tells the story in the right order. If you'd rather not think about buses and tickets, [Vesuvius and Pompeii in a day](/esperienze/vesuvio-e-pompei-in-un-giorno-con-pizza-sulle-pendici) leaves Piazza Garibaldi by coach, with entry tickets included and pizza halfway through the day. If you'd rather go on your own, read our guide to [hiking Vesuvius](/blog/trekking-vesuvio-guida) first: crater tickets are booked online and the path closes in strong wind.
Local tip: don't cram Pompeii, Herculaneum and Vesuvius into the same day. It can be done, but by evening all you'll remember is the heat. Two out of three, and save the third for your next visit.
If you'd rather have a guide

You can do Pompeii on your own, but with someone who knows it you stop looking at walls and start reading a city: who lived where, what the shops sold, what the graffiti say. The easiest option is [Pompeii with an archaeologist guide, ticket and coach from Naples](/esperienze/pompei-con-guida-archeologa-biglietto-e-pullman-da-napoli): half a day, picked up in the city and brought back, with the afternoon free.

Other visits to ruins, museums and churches are in the [Art](/categoria/arte) section. And if you want to see where everything is, from Pompeii to the centre of Naples, open the [map of Naples](/mappa): the ruins, the stations and the other day trips are all on it.

eventi-napoli-ottobre-2026.content: October in Naples is a month of its own. Daytime temperatures still reach 24°C, the sea is swimmable until mid-month and the Gaiola beach is still full on Sundays. Meanwhile the city goes back to the Neapolitans: schools have restarted, the queues for the Veiled Christ get shorter, and the tables outside stay outside. It's the best time for the things you put off in summer because it's too hot.

Below are the October 2026 events we've checked one by one, with date, time, venue and price. They're grouped by type, so you can find what you need without reading the lot. The page is updated as new dates come out, so check back.
Concerts and shows in Naples in October 2026

The month opens with the last three nights of Biagio Antonacci Unplugged at the Teatro Grande in Pompeii: 2, 3 and 4 October at 9pm, tickets online. These are acoustic concerts inside the ancient theatre of the ruins, with his familiar songs rearranged in stripped-back versions and the audience a few metres from the stage. These are the final dates.

On Sat 3 October at 9pm the Teatro Palapartenope stages Maradona, lo spettacolo: the story of Diego in Naples told through music and words, in the Fuorigrotta theatre a short walk from the stadium that bears his name. Tickets online.
The ruins by night and museums open late

The Serate nella Grande Pompei (evenings at the Pompeii sites) continue every Friday and Saturday until 10 October, 7.30pm–11.30pm, €7 per site. At Pompeii there are two routes: the one from the Amphitheatre, with the plaster casts in the Palestra Grande and the house of Giulia Felice, returns on 10 October; the other starts from the Villa dei Misteri with a shuttle to Villa Regina at Boscoreale. The walks at Villa San Marco and Villa Arianna are free. At night the ruins are something else: dark, few people, streets lit in patches.

In the city, MANN (the National Archaeological Museum) answers with MANNight: on the four Thursdays in October, the 1st, 8th, 15th and 22nd, the museum stays open 7pm–10.30pm with live music and contemporary art among the ancient statues. Tickets €10. In the evening the rooms empty out and you can take in the Farnese collection at your own pace, with no tour groups in front of the Farnese Bull.

Also at Pompeii, during normal opening hours and included in the ticket, Philip Colbert's pop-art lobsters are dotted among the Roman houses until 30 November. They divide opinion: some find them brilliant, others out of place. You can make up your own mind without spending a cent more.
Outdoors: walks, the grape harvest and the moat of Castel Sant'Elmo

The first weekend of October is packed. On Sat 3 at 4pm there's Bosco in Rosa, a four-kilometre walk at your own pace along the avenues of the Real Bosco di Capodimonte, the former royal park, in a pink T-shirt. Proceeds go to the Santobono children's hospital. Fine with pushchairs and children; registration is online.

On Sun 4 October, 9.30am–5pm, Vendemmiamo la Catalanesca takes you into the vineyards on Vesuvius where the catalanesca grape grows, once eaten only as a table grape and now made into wine. You pick in the morning, then there's a tasting and lunch among the vines. The price is announced by the organiser.

Until 4 October the Pessoa Luna Park is also open in the moat of Castel Sant'Elmo, at Via Tito Angelini 20/A in the Vomero district. It's the first time the castle moat has opened to the public: Thursday to Sunday, 5.30pm–12.30am, there are concerts, DJ sets, open-air cinema, theatre, games, chess and long shared tables. Entry €2.50, free for under-18s and over-65s. The first weekend of the month is your last chance.
Free, but book ahead

items: Tour del Giallo in the Vomero, Sat 3 and Sun 4 October, 10am–12pm: the last leg of the tour follows Maurizio de Giovanni's crime novels through the streets of the neighbourhood. Free, book by email at redazione@gialli.it.
Vespero Napoletano, the city council's slow-tourism festival: walks, workshops, concerts and roaming performances in different neighbourhoods, at weekends until 24 October. Free while places last.
The evening walks at Villa San Marco and Villa Arianna, at Stabiae, part of the Serate nella Grande Pompei: free on Fridays and Saturdays until 10 October.
eventi-napoli-ottobre-2026.content: Three things that cost nothing but need booking or getting in early:
For free events that need booking, places go fast, especially at weekends. If a date catches your eye, write the same day you see it, not on Friday evening.
With children

Every Saturday morning until 19 December there's Giro Giro Napoli: guided tours, workshops and activities for children in the city's museums and cultural sites, free. It's the simplest way to take them to a museum without hearing “when are we going home?”

Bosco in Rosa on 3 October is also designed for families: four flat kilometres, your own pace, pushchairs welcome. And the Pessoa Luna Park in the moat of Castel Sant'Elmo, until 4 October, is free for under-18s: games, chess and open-air cinema in a place that used to be off-limits. For more ideas with little ones, in any season, we have a separate guide: [things to do in Naples with kids](/blog/cosa-fare-a-napoli-con-i-bambini).
Exhibitions to see before they close

Top of the list is Maria Lai, «Essere è tessere» (“to be is to weave”), at the Museo Madre on Via Settembrini: it closes on 12 October. It's the most complete retrospective ever held in the city, sixty years of threads, fabrics, looms and sewn books, right up to the collective works that involved entire villages in Sardinia. It's worth going just to see stitching on canvas turn into drawing and storytelling at the same time. Open 10am–7.30pm, Sundays until 8pm, closed Tuesdays. Tickets €8, reduced €4.
You have longer for Philip Colbert at Pompeii, on until 30 November, but if you're going to the ruins for one of the October evenings you might as well see that too.
What to do in October when there's no event
Not every day has something in the calendar. For those, October is the right month for a few of our experiences that we don't recommend in summer.

items: The Vesuvius grape harvest, even without the event on the 4th: [Lacryma Christi among the vines, then lunch at the foot of the volcano](/esperienze/lacryma-christi-tra-i-filari-poi-a-tavola-ai-piedi-del-vulcano) takes four hours, with transport, tasting and a full lunch, €90. Up to 15 people.

The boat, while the weather holds: [three hours on a boat at sunset, with spritz and bruschetta](/esperienze/tre-ore-in-barca-al-tramonto-con-spritz-e-bruschette) leaves from the pier on Via Caracciolo, €80. In October the sun sets earlier and the sea is calmer than in August.

The underground, which at 24°C is a relief rather than a refuge: the [Galleria Borbonica](/esperienze/galleria-borbonica-cisterne-rifugi-e-auto-depoca), an hour among cisterns, air-raid shelters and vintage cars, €15, groups of up to 8.

A workshop for rainy afternoons, which start turning up in October: [Neapolitan pizza from scratch, with tiramisù to finish](/esperienze/pizza-napoletana-da-zero-con-il-tiramisu-per-finire), three hours in the historic centre, ingredients and a drink included, €50.
eventi-napoli-ottobre-2026.content: Four seasonal ideas:
If you only want one tip: do the harvest in the first half of the month and the boat in the first week. After the 15th the weather in Naples can turn overnight and boat trips start getting cancelled.
How to use this page

The events above are the ones confirmed as we write. Dates that pop up once the month has started go first on the [things to do in Naples](/cosa-fare) page, with booking links, and then here. For the coming weekend there's the short list: [things to do in Naples this weekend](/cosa-fare/weekend). If an event changes time or is cancelled, we take it off.

capri-da-napoli-in-giornata.content: Capri makes a good day trip from Naples, as long as you don't try to see everything. Just under an hour on the hydrofoil, a funicular, a bus up to Anacapri and a bit of walking: here's how to get there, what to see in a day and what time to start thinking about the way back.
Hydrofoils and ferries from Naples: where they leave from
Boats for Capri leave from two ports in Naples, right next to each other, and it pays not to mix them up.

items: Molo Beverello, opposite the Maschio Angioino castle: this is where the SNAV and NLG hydrofoils and fast boats leave. The crossing takes about fifty minutes.
Calata Porta di Massa, a few hundred metres further east: this is for the Caremar ferries, about an hour and twenty minutes, and Caremar's fast boats, around an hour.

capri-da-napoli-in-giornata.content: The ferry is slower, but it still sails when the sea is rough and the hydrofoils stay in port, and in summer you can sit out on deck. The hydrofoil saves you half an hour each way, which in a single day is a lot. Timetables change between summer and winter, with more sailings in the warmer months: check the companies' websites or the board at the ticket office the day before. All boats arrive at Marina Grande.

Local tip: buy your outward and return tickets from the same company and check the time of the last boat to Naples straight away. In October the evening sailings thin out, and missing the last hydrofoil from Capri costs you a night in a hotel on the island, at island prices.
Capri town: the funicular, the Piazzetta, the Giardini di Augusto

Get off at Marina Grande and take the funicular: a few minutes' climb through the lemon trees and you're in Piazza Umberto I, known as the Piazzetta. Buy the ticket at the bottom station. If there's a queue, and in summer there is, you can walk up a flight of steps that gets you to the same place in a good twenty minutes.

The Piazzetta is small, with café tables and the clock tower. A coffee there costs what it costs, but you drink it watching the world go by. Then take Via Vittorio Emanuele and Via Federico Serena to the Certosa di San Giacomo, a former monastery, and the Giardini di Augusto (Gardens of Augustus): flower-filled terraces with a viewpoint over the Faraglioni, the three rock stacks that are Capri's postcard. There's an entry fee; half an hour and a short walk are enough.

Below the gardens runs Via Krupp, the hairpin path cut into the rock in the early 1900s for the German industrialist Friedrich Alfred Krupp. It was closed for years because of the risk of rockfalls; these days it opens in the warmer months, this year from 1 April, and closes in autumn for maintenance on the cliff face. In late September and October check on the spot whether it's still open: if it is, walk down to Marina Piccola and swim in front of the Faraglioni.
Anacapri and the Monte Solaro chairlift

Anacapri is the other Capri: higher up, quieter, with white houses and fewer shop windows. You get there by bus from Capri or Marina Grande, a quarter of an hour of bends above the sea. Get off at Piazza Vittoria and you're already in the centre: the church of San Michele, with its majolica floor depicting the Garden of Eden, and Axel Munthe's Villa San Michele with its viewpoint.

The Monte Solaro chairlift also leaves from Piazza Vittoria, on Via Caposcuro. It's a dozen minutes on a single seat, feet dangling over gardens and vineyards, up to the summit at almost 600 metres. From up there you can see the whole island, the Faraglioni, the Sorrento coast and, when the air is clear, Vesuvius. In October it runs until the afternoon: if you want to do it, fit it in before lunch.

Local tip: eating in Anacapri costs less than in Capri, and you eat better. A plate of scialatielli ai frutti di mare (thick fresh pasta with seafood), an insalata caprese (tomato, mozzarella and basil), and you're set for the afternoon.
The Blue Grotto and a boat trip round the island

The Grotta Azzurra (Blue Grotto) is a sea cave on the north-west side of the island, with an opening so low that you can only get in lying flat in the bottom of a rowing boat. Inside, the light coming in under the waterline turns the sea a blue that doesn't look real. The Romans used it as a nymphaeum, a shrine to the water nymphs.

Two things to know. First: it only opens when the sea is calm. With a northerly wind the boatmen can't get in and the grotto stays shut, even in high summer, and nobody can tell you for sure the day before whether it will open. Second: you pay twice, for the state entry ticket, which you can book on the CoopCulture website, and for the little rowing boat that takes you in. From April to October the grotto opens at 9am and closes at 6pm. You get there by boat from Marina Grande or by bus from Anacapri, down to the steps where the boatmen wait.

If the grotto is closed, or the queue puts you off, a boat trip round the island is what makes the day. Boats from Marina Grande circle Capri in an hour or a little more: you pass beneath the Punta Carena lighthouse, through the arch of the Faraglioni, past the Grotta Verde and the Grotta Bianca (the Green and White Grottoes), below the cliffs of Villa Jovis. You see the island the way the emperors did, from the sea.

Local tip: do the Blue Grotto early in the morning, before the groups off the 9am and 10am hydrofoils arrive. If you catch one of the first boats from Naples, go straight to the boats and leave the Piazzetta for the afternoon.
When to go, and how to make it easy

Capri in August is beautiful and heaving. September and October are the right months for a day trip: the sea is still warm, the paths are quieter, the restaurants are open. From November many places close and sailings are reduced, but the island is still there. In every season the wind decides: with rough seas the hydrofoils and the Blue Grotto are off, so check the forecast the night before and have a plan B.

If you'd rather not deal with ticket offices and buses, there are two ready-made days out. [Capri and Anacapri by hydrofoil with the Gardens of Augustus](/esperienze/capri-e-anacapri-in-aliscafo-con-i-giardini-di-augusto) has the hydrofoil from Naples sorted, a minibus on the island and a guide, eight hours in all. [Capri by gozzo and on foot](/esperienze/capri-in-gozzo-e-a-piedi-giro-dellisola-anacapri-e-piazzetta) starts with an hour round the island on a gozzo, the traditional wooden boat, then Anacapri with time for the chairlift, and finishes in the Piazzetta.

If Capri is the sea day of a longer trip, our [Naples in 3 days](/blog/napoli-in-3-giorni) itinerary shows how to fit it in with everything else. Other boat trips and days out of town are in the [Outdoor](/categoria/outdoor) section, and on the [map of Naples](/mappa) you can see where Molo Beverello and Calata Porta di Massa are in relation to your hotel.

cosa-fare-a-napoli-dal-14-al-20-settembr.content: Last week Naples opened the European Volleyball Championships with Italy v Sweden in Piazza del Plebiscito, on Thu 10 at 9.05pm, tickets sold out days before. From Mon 14 the pace gets back to normal, but the calendar is full. Here's what's worth your time, day by day.
Monday 14: Verdi versus Mazzini, free in Ponticelli

At 8pm, in the Basilica di Santa Maria della Neve in Ponticelli, Enzo Decaro reads “Verdi vs Mazzini” with Samantha Sapienza, Francesco Fortes and Nadia Testa. Free entry, booking recommended. It's outside the centre, and that's exactly why you should go.

The third MANNight, the special late openings at the Museo Archeologico Nazionale (National Archaeological Museum): 7pm–11.30pm, last entry 10.30pm, evening ticket €10. From 8.30pm short performances run at the same time in the collection rooms: dance, percussion, a string quartet that moves from classical to pop, installations and DJ sets. If you'd prefer the €1 version, wait for Sat 26 September, the evening for the European Heritage Days.
Also on Thursday, at 4pm, the Nuova Orchestra Scarlatti plays at the Museum of Palaeontology in Largo San Marcellino 10, part of the Musica ai Musei series run by the Federico II University.
Friday 18: Gershwin in a courtyard and the last Unplugged
At 7.30pm, in the Cortile delle Statue at Via Paladino 39, pianist Giuseppe Gullotta and the Nuova Orchestra Scarlatti play an all-Gershwin programme. Tickets on Azzurro Service.

At 9pm (doors 8.30pm) the third edition of Napoli Unplugged, the acoustic Neapolitan music series in the Corte dell'Arte at FOQUS, Via Portacarrese a Montecalvario 69, right in the Quartieri Spagnoli (Spanish Quarter), comes to a close. On stage is Ilaria Graziano with songs from her album “Rive”. It costs €10 plus booking fee on ETES: the best value for money of the week.

From 18 to 20, at the Mostra d'Oltremare, there's also the “Il Tesoro di San Gennaro” International Chess Festival. If you play, sign up; if you don't, it's still a nice place to watch people concentrating very hard.
Saturday 19: San Gennaro, De Crescenzo and La Traviata in the courtyards

19 September is the feast of San Gennaro, the city's patron saint: at the Duomo the city waits for his blood to liquefy, as it does every year. Get there early, the cathedral fills up from the morning.

In the evening, at 9pm, Eduardo De Crescenzo brings “Essenze Jazz” to the Arena Flegrea, Viale Kennedy 54 (tickets on etes.it). On Saturday and Sunday, meanwhile, the “Traviata da Cortile” moves into the Kimbo courtyards: opera without a theatre, an arm's length from the singers.

The Certosa e Museo di San Martino brings back its Notturni in Certosa, evening visits with the view over the city from the Vomero hill. The second date is 25 September. Check times and booking on the museum's website before heading up.

items: Vespero Napoletano, the city council's slow-tourism festival: walks, workshops and concerts in the neighbourhoods until 24 October, free while places last
Giro Giro Napoli, free guided tours for children every Saturday until 19 December in museums and cultural sites
Piedigrotta Viva, six free evenings of song and storytelling in churches: 15, 16, 18, 20 and 22 September (more in our dedicated article)
cosa-fare-a-napoli-dal-14-al-20-settembr.content: Things that carry on after the 20th:
On Thursday evening, pair MANN with pizza. From Piazza Museo it's a ten-minute walk to Via dei Tribunali, and at 11.30pm the pizzerias in the centre are still open.
If you're after something to book on a set date, pick the days you're in town in the Things to do section: we'll show you the experiences available and the events on.

trekking-vesuvio-guida.content: Vesuvius is much more than a volcano. It's a symbol, an icon, a character looming over the Bay of Naples with a silhouette you can't mistake. Climbing it gets you one of the most spectacular views in Italy, but also a close-up look at the power of geology, the story of the eruption of AD 79 and the strange silence of the crater.

Contrary to what many people think, there isn't just one way to the top. The most common route starts from the car park at 1,000 metres, but there are tougher variants that start lower down and cross the old lava flows.

items: Gran Cono (the official path): about 2 hours there and back from the car park
Via Matrone: the historic route, starting from Ercolano, 4–5 hours
Sentiero Tirone: through areas of old lava, less busy and wilder
Volcanology route: with a certified guide who explains the volcano's geology

trekking-vesuvio-guida.content: When to go: seasons and times

The Vesuvius National Park is open all year, but the best times are spring (April–June) and autumn (September–October). In summer the heat can be intense and the queues at the car park long. In winter the path may close in bad weather.
The best time to reach the top is between 8am and 10am: fewer people, better light for photos and cooler temperatures.
What to put in your rucksack

items: Hiking shoes with sturdy soles (the lava ground is uneven)
At least 1.5 litres of water per person
A windproof jacket (it's always windy at the top)
Hat and sun cream
Energy snacks
Walking poles (optional but useful)

trekking-vesuvio-guida.content: Reaching the rim of the crater is hard to put into words. Below you, the crater is about 500 metres across and nearly 300 deep. Steam from the fumaroles reminds you the volcano is still active: the last eruption was in 1944. All around, the view takes in the Bay of Naples and the islands of Capri, Ischia and Procida.
Standing on the rim of Vesuvius is like standing on the border between the world of people and the world of the earth. A place that makes you feel small in the best possible way.

items: Gran Cono entry: paid ticket, book online at busy times
A certified guide is compulsory for the advanced routes
Getting there: bus from Ercolano (the Circumvesuviana station, on the local train line from Naples)
Average time: 4 hours with a guide, 2 hours for the Gran Cono alone
Dogs allowed on a lead
trekking-vesuvio-guida.content: Good to know before you set off:
Our guided Vesuvius tour includes transport from Naples, a certified volcanology guide and the entry ticket. Maximum 15 people per group.
